# Abstract {-}

**Background.** Validating a predictive biomarker requires an
interaction test. For an interaction as large as the main effect, with
two equal subgroups, it needs about four times the sample of a
main-effect test (Brookes et al. 2004).
Aggregated N-of-1 designs are
proposed to afford it,
and their power must be estimated by simulation. Hendrickson et al.
(2020) proposed a simulation method for this problem. The baseline
biomarker and three latent response components at every visit are
drawn from one multivariate normal distribution assembled from each
participant's exposure state. The predictive biomarker is a
correlation with the drug response that is present on drug and absent
off drug. We extend that data-generating process (DGP) for the Hybrid
design with carryover and judge each extension by five criteria.

**Methods.** We derive the closed-form moments and power of a
paired-difference interaction statistic under the original DGP and
the extensions. We derive a Schur-complement bound on the feasible
interaction strength. We verify them by Monte Carlo simulation,
including runs of the original code, and test fourteen analyses
against a prognostic biomarker.

**Results.** The original DGP holds the biomarker-response correlation
constant after first exposure. With any carryover the interaction is
then absent and power equals the test size. We extended the DGP so the
correlation decays at the carryover half-life. Power then returns to
its no-carryover value at half-lives of 0.1 to 0.2 week and declines
at longer ones. The decline is proved monotone for the
paired-difference statistic within each design path. For the pooled
statistic it was checked on a grid, and for the mixed model only at
the simulated half-lives. In the original code at 0.1 week, power was
`r sprintf('%.2f', m6a_p)` under the original rule (4,000 replicates)
and 0.64 with the extension, against 0.67 without carryover.
Without carryover, the original compound-symmetry structure admits no
joint distribution for correlations above 0.256. Under the original
rule with carryover the bound is higher, because the correlation then
stays constant off drug. The original effect size of 0.6 therefore
relied on repaired matrices in part of the original grid. A separable
AR(1) structure at serial
correlation 0.7 raises the bound to 0.474. A prognostic
biomarker with a pathway absent at baseline makes analyses that share
the biomarker effect with baseline anticonservative.

**Conclusions.** The correlation encoding of the interaction is
coherent. It needs a decaying correlation, a correlation structure
with room for realistic effects, and a feasibility check that stops
instead of repairing. We give the closed-form results, the code
changes, the extended DGP and planning sample sizes.

**Trial registration.** Not applicable.

**Keywords:** N-of-1 trials; predictive biomarker; simulation;
carryover; data-generating process; power; prazosin.

# Background

Validating a predictive biomarker requires a biomarker-by-treatment
interaction test [@sargent2005]. When the interaction is as large as
the main effect and divides the sample into two equal subgroups, such a
test needs about four times the sample of the main-effect test
[@brookes2004]. Aggregated N-of-1 designs are proposed as the way to
afford it. Their power must be estimated by simulation. Hendrickson et
al. [@hendrickson2020] proposed a simulation method for this problem.
We found no precedent for it in the N-of-1 literature we searched
(below). The
baseline biomarker and, at every visit, three latent response
components are drawn from one multivariate normal distribution. The
trial design assembles the correlation matrix from each participant's
exposure state. The predictive biomarker is a correlation with the
drug response that is present on drug and absent off drug. We call
this process the original DGP. This paper extends it for the Hybrid
design, which combines open-label titration, blinded discontinuation
and a brief crossover, with carryover between phases. The extensions
address two limits of the original DGP. Under any carryover the
original DGP has no interaction to detect. Its largest effect size has
no valid joint distribution. The paper adds a correlation that decays
after discontinuation and a feasibility check. It decides the elements
the original DGP left open. It ends with the extended DGP and the
sample sizes it implies.

## Aggregated N-of-1 trials and predictive biomarkers

In an aggregated N-of-1 trial each participant moves between drug and
placebo, or between drug and no drug, several times. The individual
series are analyzed together [@nikles2011; @vohra2016cent; @punja2016].
Every participant contributes both an on-drug and an off-drug
response. The design can therefore estimate how the drug effect varies
between people. It can then test whether a baseline measurement
predicts who benefits [@senn2016mastering; @schork2015]. The motivating
example is prazosin for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Prazosin has been tested in several randomized trials
[@raskind2003; @raskind2013; @raskind2018]. The largest, the VA
Cooperative Studies Program trial CSP 563 (304 veterans), found no
benefit on its primary outcomes [@raskind2018]. In a secondary
analysis of an earlier trial in 67 soldiers, higher pretreatment
standing systolic blood pressure was associated with greater symptom
reduction on prazosin but not on placebo, about 14 points on the
Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale per 10 mm Hg [@raskind2016bp].
Blood pressure was therefore proposed as a candidate predictive
biomarker. That association did not replicate in our reanalysis of
CSP 563 (`docs/69` of the repository; participant-level data not
public). In 279 participants the arm-by-blood-pressure interaction was
+0.25 points per 10 mm Hg (95% CI $-2.72$ to 3.21), which excludes
the published value. Prazosin and blood pressure therefore serve here
as a worked example for the units of the planning section, not as an
established predictive biomarker.

Closed-form power calculations exist only for simplified versions of
these designs [@wang2019; @senn2002]. Power is therefore estimated by
simulating trials from a data-generating process (DGP) and analyzing
each simulated trial [@morris2019simulation]. Several simulators of
N-of-1 and aggregated N-of-1 data exist. Percha et al. [@percha2019]
simulate single series with exponential wash-in and wash-out to choose
block lengths and sampling rates. Chen and Chen [@chen2014] generate
cycles under compound symmetry or AR(1) with a carryover effect to
compare analyses. Blackston et al. [@blackston2019] and Gärtner et al.
[@gartner2023] simulate aggregated series with carryover to compare
designs and estimators. None of these four represents a baseline
biomarker that modifies the drug response. Grenet et al. [@grenet2020] simulate
crossover and parallel-group trials with a binary predictive biomarker.
They encode it as a mean-term interaction. In single-case research,
multilevel models with moderators of the intervention effect are
established [@vandennoortgate2003; @moeyaert2014], and Moeyaert et al.
[@moeyaert2022power] estimate by simulation the power to detect such a
moderator. There, too, the moderator enters the mean model. The DGP
determines what a simulation
can show: how the biomarker interaction is represented, how the drug
effect builds and wanes, and how carryover from one period reaches the
next.

## The original DGP

The original DGP has three parts. The first is a component
decomposition of the symptom score. The score is the baseline level
minus three responses. Each response follows a modified Gompertz
curve. The drug-response component (BR) is driven by time since the
current on-drug period began. The placebo-response component (PB) is
driven by time in the trial and scaled by the participant's
expectancy, the probability of receiving drug given the design. The
natural-history component (TV) is driven by time in the trial. The
second part is the design specification for open-label, crossover,
blinded-discontinuation and Hybrid designs. It tracks time on drug,
time since discontinuation and expectancy at each visit. The third
part is open software (the `pmsimstats` R package).

The original DGP also encodes the predictive biomarker in a
distinctive way. Statistical models and sample-size methods for N-of-1
and crossover designs usually represent treatment-effect heterogeneity
as random participant-by-treatment variation
[@senn2016mastering; @araujo2016; @senn2019samplesize; @zucker1997].
The original DGP instead places the biomarker in the same multivariate
normal distribution as the response components. The biomarker has a
nonzero correlation $c_{bm}$ with the drug response at on-drug visits.
Without carryover it has zero correlation elsewhere. We call $c_{bm}$
the biomarker-response correlation. A predictive biomarker is then one
whose association with the outcome differs between on-drug and
off-drug visits. The parameterization keeps the marginal distribution
of the drug response fixed. It expresses the strength of the
interaction as a correlation. We call this the correlation encoding of
the interaction.

The statement that the encoding has no precedent rests on three
database searches. On 2026-10-27 we searched PubMed for (N-of-1 OR
single patient OR aggregated N-of-1) AND simulation AND (biomarker OR
effect modifier OR treatment-by-covariate) AND (power OR sample size).
It returned one record, the original study. On 2026-11-03 we searched
PubMed titles and abstracts for ("N-of-1" OR "single-patient" OR
"single-case" OR "aggregated N-of-1" OR crossover) AND (simulation OR
simulated OR "Monte Carlo") AND (biomarker OR moderator OR "effect
modifier" OR "treatment-by-covariate") AND (power OR "sample size").
We ran the same terms, without "Monte Carlo", against abstracts in
Europe PMC. Both returned two records: the original study and a
simulation of moderator power in single-case multilevel models
[@moeyaert2022power]. Neither search retrieved Grenet et al.
[@grenet2020], which we identified otherwise, so the searches are not
exhaustive. Web of Science and Scopus were not searched.
The searches cover the N-of-1, crossover and single-case literature
indexed in these two databases. They do not cover the wider
literature on joint simulation of covariates and outcomes, such as
copula methods. The claim is therefore limited to the N-of-1
literature we searched.

## Why the joint distribution is built from the design

The simplest DGP that could serve would generate one symptom score per
visit. Its mean would carry the design effects and an interaction term
$\beta\, B_i D_{it}$. Its residual would be compound symmetric or
AR(1). Most simulators of crossover and N-of-1 data use that form
[@chen2014; @wang2019], and the analysis model
assumes it. It is adequate when the question is the main effect. It is
not adequate for the questions this series asks, for four reasons.

1. **Carryover would be whatever the analyst specifies.** In the
   simple form carryover is a mean shift added at off-drug visits.
   Whether the design still identifies the interaction under carryover
   depends on how the biomarker's association with the response
   persists after discontinuation. The simple form has no such
   association, so the question cannot be studied.
2. **The interaction would be only a conditional mean effect.** With
   a mean term the residual variance of the drug response is the same
   at every biomarker value. A predictive biomarker that explains part
   of the between-person variation in drug response implies a
   responder class in the population. That implies a correlation
   between the biomarker and the drug response. The simple form has no
   parameter for it (Appendix A.6).
3. **A prognostic pathway could not be generated.** A biomarker may
   also be associated with the placebo response or with the natural
   history of the condition. Such a biomarker enters the observed
   outcome through a pathway the analysis cannot see. Whether an
   analysis keeps its nominal size under that feature can only be
   tested by a DGP that generates the pathways separately.
4. **Existence and identifiability would be invisible.** In the simple
   form every parameter combination yields a valid distribution. The
   design enters only through the regressor pattern. Whether the
   simulated effect sizes are jointly possible, and how much of the
   interaction the design can see, are questions about the joint
   distribution of the biomarker and the response components. They
   have closed-form answers only when that distribution is specified.

The original DGP specifies it. The biomarker and the three response
components at every visit form one multivariate normal vector. The
design assembles its correlation matrix. The biomarker is correlated
with the drug response at on-drug visits, and at a value set by the
exposure state at off-drug visits. The components are serially
correlated in calendar weeks. The components are cross-correlated
through a common block. Three results follow. The largest feasible
interaction is a property of the design, not a number found by trial
and error. We call it the feasibility bound. The power of a
paired-difference statistic has a closed form. The design enters it
through the on/off correlation difference, the on-drug correlation
minus the mean off-drug correlation. The residual structure the
analysis model should assume can be derived from the DGP. Three
requirements come with this form. The marginal
covariance of the outcome is implied rather than chosen. The joint
distribution must exist. Every entry must be calibrated or declared
uncalibrated. The Discussion shows that, conditional on the biomarker,
the correlation encoding reduces to the mean-term form with a smaller
residual variance, so the standard form remains available within it.

The DGP is not new in its parts. Simulating repeated measures from a
multivariate normal with compound symmetry or AR(1) and a carryover
term is routine [@chen2014; @wang2019]. Decomposing a clinical
trajectory into disease progression, placebo response and drug action
is the pharmacometric convention [@holford2015]. Separable (Kronecker)
covariances for several response variables measured repeatedly are an
established model [@galecki1994]. The original DGP combined these
parts. It placed a baseline variable in the joint distribution of the
latent response components, with a correlation indexed by each visit's
exposure state. Designs for heterogeneity analyses in cluster
randomized trials also use correlations of an effect modifier, but
these are intraclass correlations of the modifier and of the outcome,
and the modification itself is a term in the mean model [@li2023].
This paper extends
that combination. We found no other instance of it in the N-of-1
literature we searched (above).

## What a data-generating process for these trials must satisfy

Reusing the original DGP for a series of simulation studies showed
where it could be extended. To judge an extension, a criterion for
"better" is needed. We use five. Each stage of the Results ends with
the choice made and the criterion it rests on.

1. **Existence.** The joint distribution must exist for the effect
   sizes a study simulates. The correlation matrix must be positive
   definite. We measure this by the largest feasible $c_{bm}$ (the
   feasibility bound) and by the number of matrices a grid would need
   to repair.
2. **Identifiability under carryover.** The biomarker-by-treatment
   interaction must remain a contrast between on-drug and off-drug
   visits when carryover is present. We measure this by the on/off
   correlation difference. The closed form shows that this difference
   governs power.
3. **Fidelity to the pharmacology.** The time course of the drug
   effect, its decay after discontinuation and its behavior at
   re-exposure should be consistent with a short-half-life, titrated
   drug such as prazosin. This is a judgment. We state it as such
   where it decides a stage.
4. **Analyzability.** The residual structure the DGP generates should
   be one the analysis model can represent. The DGP should also be
   able to generate the features that decide which analyses are valid,
   such as a prognostic biomarker. We measure this by the agreement of
   the generated residual structure with the analysis model's, and by
   null rejection rates under those features.
5. **Calibration status.** Every parameter should be labeled as the
   original value, a choice made here, or uncalibrated. The DGP's
   values have not been re-estimated for this paper. A reanalysis of
   CSP 563 (planning section) estimates some quantities on the total
   symptom score and shows that others are not identifiable from a
   parallel-group trial. This criterion is therefore reported, not
   met.

A DGP meeting criteria 1 to 4, with criterion 5 reported, is what we
call the extended DGP. Its label in the repository's code and data is
`refined`.

**The reference drug.** Prazosin's plasma half-life is about 2.3 hours
[@hobbs1978], against weekly visits. The plasma concentration
therefore falls by orders of magnitude within a day of the last dose.
We assume a symptom-level half-life of 0.1 to 0.2 week (17 to 34
hours), or 7 to 15 plasma half-lives, as the pharmacological range.
No symptom-response half-life for prazosin in PTSD has been reported,
so the range is an assumption. The Results
therefore cover 0 to 2 weeks and label half-lives of 0.5 week and
above as behavioral scenarios. The drug is re-titrated after an
interruption, which bears on how the DGP treats re-exposure (Stage 3).

## Aims

This paper extends the original DGP and judges each extension against
the five criteria. The Hybrid design is the primary case. The
open-label, blinded-discontinuation and crossover designs are
comparators. The paper shows in closed form why power equals the test
size under the original DGP when carryover is present, and why its
joint distribution often does not exist. It gives the changes to the
original code that add a decaying correlation and a feasibility check.
It chooses, with reasons, the elements the original DGP leaves open.
It collects the result as a reference specification with the stage
that justifies each element. It gives the sample sizes a trialist
needs to plan an aggregated N-of-1 trial under it.

# Methods

The Methods describe the original DGP and the tools used to judge each
extension: the estimands, a statistic with a closed-form distribution,
the feasibility bound and the simulation studies. Every choice about
the DGP is made in the Results.

## The original data-generating process

We use the original DGP's notation, with a few additions. Participant
$i$ is observed at a baseline visit $t = 0$ and at post-baseline visits
$t = 1, \ldots, T$, at calendar weeks $w_t$ (4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 16
and 20 in the Hybrid design). The symptom score is

$$
Y_{it} = \mathrm{BL}_i - \left(TV_{it} + PB_{it} + BR_{it}\right),
$$

so a larger response lowers the score. Each component has a mean given
by the modified Gompertz curve

$$
G(x;\, m, d, r) = m\,\frac{\exp(-d e^{-rx}) - e^{-d}}{1 - e^{-d}},
$$

which the code obtains by subtracting the offset $m e^{-d}$ from
$m\exp(-d e^{-rx})$ and rescaling, so that $G(0) = 0$ and
$G(\infty) = m$. It is evaluated at a component-specific clock:

- The drug-response component (BR) at time on drug $t_{od}$, the time
  since the current on-drug period began, with $m = 10.99$, $d = 5$,
  $r = 0.42$ and SD 8. The curve reaches its inflection at 3.8 weeks,
  half its maximum at 4.7 weeks and 90% at 9.2 weeks.
- The placebo-response component (PB) at time in the trial, scaled by
  the expectancy $\eta_t$ (1 in the open-label phase, 0.5 when
  blinded), with $m = 6.51$, $d = 5$, $r = 0.35$ and SD $10\eta_t$.
- The natural-history component (TV) at time in the trial, with the
  same curve as PB and SD 10.

The biomarker has mean 124.3 and SD 15.4, and baseline severity has
mean 83.1 and SD 18.5. These are the values of the original code's
parameter objects at commit 58b32a9, stored in the package as
`extracted_rp` and `extracted_bp`. Every simulation and closed-form
calculation in this paper uses them, including the simulations of the
analysis G10 in the planning section and the paired rerun of Appendix
B.4. In those two, the biomarker enters the analysis standardized to
mean 0 and SD 1, so their interaction coefficients are per SD of
biomarker; the standardization is linear and does not change the test.

Off drug, the drug-response mean decays from its previous value with
half-life $t_{1/2}$:
$\mu_{BR,t} = \mu_{BR,t-1}\, 2^{-t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}}$, where $t_{sd}$ is
the time since discontinuation. We call this the original carryover
rule. When the drug is resumed, time on drug restarts at zero.

The vector (biomarker, baseline, $TV_{i\cdot}$, $PB_{i\cdot}$,
$BR_{i\cdot}$) is multivariate normal. Within each component the
correlation between any two visits is $\rho_{cs} = 0.8$ (compound
symmetry). We write $\rho_{cs}$ to keep $\rho$ for the AR(1)
correlation per week. Between components the correlation is
$c_1 = 0.2$ at the same visit and $c_\times = 0.1$ otherwise. The
biomarker's correlation with $BR_{it}$ is $c_{bm}\,g_t$, where $g_t$
is the correlation profile, the fraction of $c_{bm}$ present at visit
$t$. The original rule sets $g_t = 1$ wherever the drug-response mean
is nonzero and 0 elsewhere. The correlation is therefore constant
after first exposure. When the correlation matrix is not positive
definite, the covariance matrix built from it is not either, and the
original code replaces that covariance matrix with a nearby
positive-definite one (`corpcor::make.positive.definite` with
tolerance $10^{-3}$, which follows Higham's nearest symmetric
positive semidefinite matrix [@higham1988] and raises every
eigenvalue below $2 \times 10^{-3}$ to that value). The repair changes
the variances as well as the correlations. No warning is issued.

The original analysis is the linear mixed model

$$
Y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_B B_i + \beta_D D_{it} + \beta_T w_t
  + \beta_{bm:D} B_i D_{it} + u_i + \varepsilon_{it},
$$

with a random intercept $u_i$, the binary drug indicator $D_{it}$, and
baseline included as a row with $D_{i0} = 0$. The interaction
$\beta_{bm:D}$ is tested with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
[@kuznetsova2017]. Participants are assigned to the design's paths in
fixed numbers (18, 18, 17 and 17 in the Hybrid design at $N = 70$),
not at random.

## Estimands

The target is the on-drug biomarker moderation of the drug response.
This is the change in the drug effect per unit of biomarker while the
drug is fully present. Without carryover it equals
$\beta_{bm:D} = -c_{bm}\sigma_{BR}/\sigma_{bm}$.

Analyses that contrast on-drug with off-drug visits through a binary
drug indicator estimate this quantity only when no moderation remains
off drug. Under carryover they estimate an attenuated on-minus-off
contrast. Analyses with an exposure-decayed indicator $D_{bc,it}$ at
the true half-life recover the on-drug moderation. At another analysis
half-life, fixed or chosen from the data, they recover it only
approximately. Table
\@ref(tab:estimands) states which analysis in this paper targets which
quantity. The three sets of results are compared only where their
targets coincide (no carryover) or where the attenuation is the object
of study (Stage 2).

Table: (\#tab:estimands) The analyses used in this paper and the quantity each estimates.

| Analysis | Drug indicator | Estimates | Used in |
|----------------------------|------------------|--------------------------------------|--------------|
| Paired-difference statistic E9, E9b (closed form) | binary | on-minus-off contrast, $\beta_{bm:D}$ times the on/off correlation difference | Stages 1, 2, 4, 5; planning |
| The original analysis (mixed model) | binary | the same contrast | Stage 2 (original code) |
| Stress test: the original analysis | binary | the on-minus-off contrast | Stage 6 |
| Stress test: fixed-half-life analyses | $D_{bc,it}$ at an analysis half-life of 0.5 week, the true half-life except in the cells that vary it | on-drug moderation $\beta_{bm:D}$ where the half-lives match | Stage 6 |
| Stress test: analyses with the half-life chosen by AIC | $D_{bc,it}$ at the AIC-chosen half-life (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1 or 2 weeks) | on-drug moderation $\beta_{bm:D}$ where the chosen half-life is the true one | Stage 6 |

## The paired-difference statistic

To isolate how carryover acts, we use a summary statistic whose
distribution can be derived exactly (Appendix A). For each participant,

$$
\Delta_i = \bar Y_i^{\text{on}} - \bar Y_i^{\text{off}}
  = \sum_t a_t Y_{it},
$$

the difference between the mean on-drug and mean off-drug scores. It
is regressed on $B_i$ by least squares. We call it E9 when it uses
post-baseline visits only. We call it E9b when baseline is counted as
one more off-drug visit, as in the original analysis. In the Hybrid
design, Monte Carlo simulation of the original mixed model shows that
E9b reproduces its mean estimates to within 0.004. It reproduces its
power closely (0.654 against 0.632 without carryover). In the
crossover design the closed form understates the mixed model's power
(0.645 against 0.708 without carryover, and 0.279 against 0.31 to 0.35
under the original rule). The mixed model's time term uses the
between-path contrast that the paired difference discards. The
derivation gives three results.

- **Proposition 1.** The variance of $\Delta$ does not depend on the
  carryover half-life. The half-life enters only through the response
  means and the correlation profile. Neither appears in the variance.
- **Proposition 2.** The population slope is
  $$
  \beta_{bm:D}^{\text{E9}}
    = -c_{bm}\frac{\sigma_{BR}}{\sigma_{bm}}\left(1 - \bar g_{\text{off}}\right),
  \qquad
  \beta_{bm:D}^{\text{E9b}}
    = -c_{bm}\frac{\sigma_{BR}}{\sigma_{bm}}
      \left(1 - \frac{n_{\text{off}}}{n_{\text{off}} + 1}\,
      \bar g_{\text{off}}\right),
  $$
  where $\bar g_{\text{off}}$ is the mean of $g_t$ over the
  $n_{\text{off}}$ post-baseline off-drug visits. The slopes are
  specific to each path. In the Hybrid design $n_{\text{off}}$ is 3 in
  two paths and 4 in the other two. The pooled slope is their
  allocation-weighted average.
- **Power** is a noncentral-$t$ probability governed by the correlation
  $r_{\Delta B}$ between $\Delta$ and $B$. For E9 that correlation is
  proportional to the on/off correlation difference
  $\mathcal G = 1 - \bar g_{\text{off}}$. For E9b it is proportional to
  $1 - \frac{n_{\text{off}}}{n_{\text{off}}+1}\bar g_{\text{off}}$.

So carryover can affect power only through the on/off correlation
difference. The propositions reduce the question of why power falls
to the question of what the correlation rule does to
$\bar g_{\text{off}}$.

## The feasibility bound

Write the response block of the correlation matrix as $M$ and the
biomarker's correlations with the response components as
$c_{bm}\tilde g$, with $\tilde g$ the correlation profile padded with
zeros at the $TV$ and $PB$ entries. The full matrix is positive
definite if and only if $M$ is, and

$$
c_{bm}^2\, \tilde g^\top M^{-1} \tilde g < 1 .
$$

The left side is the squared multiple correlation of the biomarker on
the whole response trajectory. The largest feasible $c_{bm}$, the
feasibility bound, is therefore
$c_{bm}^{\ast} = (\tilde g^\top M^{-1} \tilde g)^{-1/2}$ (Appendix A.4).
It depends on the correlation structure, the design and the
correlation profile. It is a bound on the DGP, not on any analysis.

## Simulation studies

We designed and report the simulations following the ADEMP structure
of Morris et al. [@morris2019simulation]: aims, data-generating
mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures. There are
three studies (Table \@ref(tab:ademp)). The scripts are listed under
Availability of data and materials. The closed-form calculations of
Stages 4 and 5 and of the planning section use the same code as study
1 with $\rho$ varied. A fourth run, described in the planning section,
simulates the analysis G10 of the companion paper
[@pmsimstats-paper02] under the extended DGP with the original
parameters. It supplies the G10 columns of the planning tables, the
G10 sample sizes for 80 percent power and the G10 panel of Figure 4B
(Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bg10)). Its generator reproduces the closed-form
power of E9 within two Monte Carlo SEs in the Hybrid, OL+BDC and
crossover designs ($N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, $t_{1/2} = 0.2$ week,
1,000 replicates; `42-check-param-sets.R`).

Table: (\#tab:ademp) Design of the three simulation studies in the
ADEMP structure. MCSE: Monte Carlo standard error of a rejection rate,
$\sqrt{p(1-p)/R}$ for $R$ replicates.

| | 1. Closed-form verification | 2. The original code | 3. Stress test under a prognostic biomarker |
|--------------|------------------------------|------------------------------|------------------------------|
| **Aim** | Check the closed-form moments and power of Appendix A, and the loss of power under the original rule | Show on the original code that the correlation rule alone determines the loss of power | Find which analyses keep their nominal size under features the extended DGP adds |
| **Data-generating mechanisms** | The correlation encoding with the original rule and with the decaying correlation; compound symmetry and the separable AR(1) form; carryover on the drug-response mean decaying from the last on-drug value; Hybrid, crossover and OL+BDC designs; $N = 70$; grids of $c_{bm}$ and $t_{1/2}$ | The original `generateData()` at commit 58b32a9, as published and with the decaying correlation only (Appendix B.1); $c_{bm} = 0.25$. (a) Hybrid, $N = 70$, no censoring, $t_{1/2} \in \{0, 0.1, 0.2, 1\}$; (b) four designs, $N \in \{35, 70\}$, $t_{1/2} \in \{0, 0.1, 0.2\}$, the original censoring patterns | The extended DGP (Table \@ref(tab:spec)), with randomized allocation (the first run: fixed allocation and the original carryover rule); base cell separable AR(1), $\rho = 0.7$, $N = 70$, $t_{1/2} = 0.5$ week; 15 null cells (11 without and 4 with a prognostic pathway of strength 0.3) and 10 alternative cells at $c_{bm} = 0.30$ varying $N$, half-life, decay form, dropout and measurement error |
| **Estimand** | $\beta_{bm:D}$, and the mean of the paired-difference statistic | $\beta_{bm:D}$ | $\beta_{bm:D}$ |
| **Methods** | Paired-difference statistics E9 and E9b, closed form and simulated; the original mixed model fitted with `lmer` | The original analysis pipeline (`lmer`, model-based test) on both versions | Fourteen analyses fitted to the same simulated trials; two-sided tests at $\alpha = 0.05$ |
| **Performance measures** | Mean, SD and power of the statistic; agreement as (simulated $-$ closed form)/MCSE | Power; mean interaction estimate; number of repaired correlation matrices | Null rejection rate; power; $\kappa$, the ratio of mean model SE to empirical SD; failed fits |
| **Replicates** | 5,000 per cell (MCSE of power at most 0.007); 500 to 1,000 for `lmer` | (a) 500 per cell (MCSE at most 0.022); (b) 250 per cell (at most 0.032) | 1,000 per null cell (MCSE 0.0069 at a rate of 0.05), 500 per alternative cell (at most 0.022) |

```{r cfcount}
## Study 1 agreement count: every cell-variant of the closed-form
## check (01-e9-closed-form.R), all designs and structures.
cfz <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                          'carryover-closed-form', 'e9-closed-form-vs-mc.csv'))
cf_n <- nrow(cfz)
cf_beyond <- sum(abs(cfz$power_z) > 2)
cf_expect <- round(cf_n * 2 * pnorm(-2))
```

**Number of replicates.** Replicate counts were set by the precision
each comparison needs. In study 3, 1,000 null replicates give a
two-MCSE band of 0.036 to 0.064 for a single cell. Pooling 11
non-prognostic null cells gives the band of 0.046 to 0.054 used in
Stage 6. In study 1, a cell is flagged when the simulated and
closed-form values differ by more than 2 MCSE. Chance alone produces
this in about 4.6% of cells, or about `r cf_expect` of the `r cf_n`
cell-variants (three designs, three correlation structures, two
statistics); `r cf_beyond` were flagged. The cell-variants are not
independent, since each uses its own draws but the same designs.

**Random numbers.** Every cell, or chunk of a cell, sets its own seed
from a fixed rule: a function of the cell's parameters in study 1, a
shared seed per half-life (study 2a) or per design, sample size and
half-life (study 2b), and $20261007 + 1000 \times \text{cell} +
\text{chunk}$ in study 3. Results therefore do not depend on the
number of cores or the order in which chunks run. Both versions of the
original code in study 2 use the same seeds. All analyses in study 3
are fitted to the same trials. The comparisons are therefore paired.
R's default Mersenne-Twister generator was used throughout.

**Failed fits and repaired matrices.** In study 3, a fit that returned
an error was recorded as missing. In the second run, failures numbered
0 to 7 per analysis over 28,000 trials, and at most 0.4% in any cell.
In the first run they numbered 0 to 12, and at most 0.6% in any cell.
In study 2
the original pipeline returned an estimate for every replicate. No
correlation matrix was repaired in either version, because
$c_{bm} = 0.25$ lies below the compound-symmetry feasibility bound of
0.256. Study 1 does not fit models for the paired-difference
statistic, so it has no failures.

**Which form of the DGP each study used.** Study 1 and the closed-form
calculations build the cross-component correlation as
$c_1\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$ (the separable form) where the
separable structure is named, and as the original constants where
compound symmetry is named. Study 2 is the original code and so the
original structure. Study 3 was run twice with the separable form.
The first run used fixed path allocation (18, 18, 17, 17) and the
original carryover rule on the mean. The second run used carryover
decaying from the last on-drug mean, the rule of the extended DGP. It
also assigned each participant to a path at random in every trial.
The second run therefore changed two things at once. The stored
outputs contain no run that changes only one of them, so their
effects cannot be separated. The tables in Stage 6 are from the second
run. The first run is in Appendix C, Table \@ref(tab:prognosticfirst).
Randomized allocation is a driver option, not part of the extended
DGP as defined (Table \@ref(tab:spec)).

**Software.** R 4.6.1, with lme4 2.0.1 and lmerTest 3.2.1 for the
original pipeline, nlme 3.1-169, mmrm 0.3.17, clubSandwich 0.7.0 and
MASS 7.3-65.

**Exploratory status.** The stress test is exploratory. Its cells and
analyses were written down as a working protocol in `docs/46` of the
repository. No analysis plan was fixed in advance, and the protocol
was revised as results came in. Two cells with a prognostic
association between the biomarker and baseline severity, and three
analyses, were added after the first results. Failed fits were first
counted as non-rejections and are now excluded from the denominator,
a change of at most 0.0025 in any rate. The study also compared the
analyses' power and selected one by a decision rule. That selection
was revised after results, is post hoc, and is reported in the
project's documentation (`docs/56`), not here. This paper uses the
stress test only for what it shows about the DGP: which analyses are
valid under a prognostic biomarker, and what the optional features do
to size and power.

# Results

The Results are organized as stages. Each stage states what the
original DGP does, what the extension adds, the evidence, and the
choice made with the criterion it rests on. Table \@ref(tab:spec), at
the end, collects the choices.

## Stage 1. Validity of the joint distribution

The original DGP accepts any $c_{bm}$ and repairs a correlation matrix
that is not positive definite. Under its compound-symmetry structure
the matrix is positive definite only for $c_{bm}$ below a bound.
Without carryover the bound is 0.256 in the Hybrid design (0.256 in
the crossover and 0.262 in the open-label-plus-blinded-discontinuation
design). These values follow from the feasibility bound with $M$ the
original response block. The nonzero effect sizes in the original
study were 0.3 and 0.6. Counting one matrix per design path, effect
size and half-life, 37% of the original grid's matrices at those
effect sizes (20 of 54) were replaced by nearby valid matrices (Table
\@ref(tab:nonpd)). At $c_{bm} = 0.3$ the repair changed no correlation
by more than 0.007. The original results at that effect size are
therefore essentially those of the stated DGP. At $c_{bm} = 0.6$ the
repair lowered the on-drug correlation to 0.54 to 0.57 and moved other
correlations by up to 0.10. Those results describe a different DGP
from the one stated.

The bound is the condition that the biomarker's squared multiple
correlation on the whole response trajectory stays below one. Under
compound symmetry every visit's drug response shares the same
person-level factor. The biomarker therefore cannot be correlated with
the on-drug visits alone without being correlated, through that
factor, with the off-drug visits as well. The bound is low because the
correlation profile switches between visits that the structure ties
together.

We extended the DGP to check feasibility and stop. When the matrix is
not positive definite, the extended DGP reports the cell as infeasible
instead of changing it (Appendix B.2). The package function
`buildSigma()` now does so by default (Appendix B.5). The choice rests
on the existence criterion. One consequence is that the original
effect size of 0.6 cannot be simulated under any correlation encoding
in this paper. Table \@ref(tab:nonpd) shows it infeasible in 75% of
the extended grid under the extended DGP, and in every Hybrid cell.
The original DGP passes those cells at positive half-lives because its
rule keeps the correlation constant after first exposure. A constant
correlation places a small demand on the structure, and it carries no
interaction (Stage 2). The cells that need no repair under the
original rule are the cells in which the interaction is absent. What
the bound means in outcome units, and what to do above it, are taken
up in the planning section and the Discussion.

The case that fixed the default was a prognostic scenario in the
companion study [@pmsimstats-paper02], not the original grid. Two runs
combined $c_{bm} = 0.45$ with a prognostic correlation of 0.6. The
joint bound of Stage 6 shows that combination to be infeasible at any
$c_{bm}$. The repair lowered the on-drug correlation, and the runs
reported the attenuated interaction as a loss of power to the
prognostic pathway. A repaired matrix does not report which
correlation it changed. A repair therefore turns an infeasible input
into a plausible but wrong finding. One degenerate case is
distinguished from a failure of existence. The placebo-response
component has standard deviation proportional to the expectancy. A
visit with expectancy zero has exactly zero placebo-response variance
and makes the covariance matrix singular by construction. The stop
path factors only the positive-variance sub-block and draws the
degenerate components at their means. No correlation is changed
(Appendix B.2).

```{r nonpd}
tab <- data.frame(
  grid = c('Figure 4 grid of the original study, $c_{bm} \\in \\{0, 0.3, 0.6\\}$ (81)',
           'Extended grid, $c_{bm} = 0.25$ (40)', 'Extended grid, $c_{bm} = 0.3$ (40)',
           'Extended grid, $c_{bm} = 0.6$ (40)'),
  orig = c('20 (25\\%)', '0 (0\\%)', '12 (30\\%)', '12 (30\\%)'),
  ref8 = c('21 (26\\%)', '0 (0\\%)', '0 (0\\%)', '30 (75\\%)'),
  ref7 = c('21 (26\\%)', '0 (0\\%)', '0 (0\\%)', '30 (75\\%)'))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE,
  col.names = c('Grid (number of matrices)',
                'Original DGP (constant correlation, compound symmetry, $\\rho_{cs} = 0.8$)',
                'Extended DGP (decaying correlation, separable AR(1)), $\\rho = 0.8$',
                'Extended DGP, $\\rho = 0.7$'),
  caption = 'Correlation matrices that are not positive definite. Figure 4 grid: open label, open label plus blinded discontinuation, crossover and Hybrid designs; $t_{1/2} \\in \\{0, 0.1, 0.2\\}$ week. Extended grid: the last three designs; $t_{1/2} \\in \\{0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1\\}$ week. The original-DGP counts reproduce those of the original code exactly. The extended-DGP counts are the same at $\\rho = 0.7$ (the recommended value) and $\\rho = 0.8$ because both feasibility bounds lie between 0.3 and 0.6.') |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = '4.6cm') |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(2:4, width = '2.9cm')
```

## Stage 2. The biomarker-response correlation under carryover

The original study reported that power to detect the interaction fell
sharply once carryover was introduced. In our 500-replicate rerun of
the original code in the Hybrid design at $N = 70$ and
$c_{bm} = 0.25$ (Table \@ref(tab:patch)), power fell from 0.668 without
carryover to 0.126 at a half-life of 0.1 week; a 4,000-replicate rerun
of that cell gives `r sprintf('%.3f', m6a_p)` (below). No correlation
matrix
was repaired in that run, because 0.25 lies below the
compound-symmetry feasibility bound of 0.256. At that half-life only
0.1% of the drug effect remains a week after stopping.
Figure 4 of the original study shows the same pattern. We did not
read values off it.

Under the original rule every off-drug visit in the Hybrid design
follows an exposure. With any positive half-life its drug-response
mean is positive, so $g_t = 1$. Hence $\bar g_{\text{off}} = 1$ and,
by Proposition 2,

$$
\beta_{bm:D}^{\text{E9}} = 0, \qquad
\beta_{bm:D}^{\text{E9b}} = -c_{bm}\frac{\sigma_{BR}}{\sigma_{bm}}\,
  \frac{1}{n_{\text{off}} + 1}
\qquad \text{for every } t_{1/2} > 0 .
$$

Power is a step function of the half-life (Table
\@ref(tab:closedform), Figure \@ref(fig:powerfig)). It takes its
no-carryover value at $t_{1/2} = 0$. It takes a constant value at
every positive half-life of practical interest, whether 0.1 week or
10. The exception below about 0.007 week is an artifact of
double-precision arithmetic in the original code, not a property of
the DGP (Appendix B.1). For E9b the constant is 0.081. This value
comes from the baseline row, which alone keeps $g_t = 0$.

```{r m6data}
m6 <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                         'hendrickson-problems', 'graded-patch',
                         'published-th0.1-reps4000.csv'))
m6_R <- sum(m6$reps)
m6_p <- sum(m6$rej) / m6_R
m6_se <- sqrt(m6_p * (1 - m6_p) / m6_R)
stopifnot(m6_R == 4000, all(m6$t_half == 0.1), sum(m6$repairs) == 0)
```

The original analysis behaves the same way. In our reconstruction of
the original DGP, the mean estimate falls from $-0.126$ to between
$-0.026$ and $-0.032$ at every positive half-life. Power falls from
0.63 to between 0.08 and 0.11 (500 replicates per cell). The
separately seeded run of the original code reported above gives 0.126
at 0.1 week, against 0.080 for the reconstruction. The difference is
2.4 combined Monte Carlo SE (two-sided $p = 0.016$). The two
implementations share the parameters, the path allocation and the
analysis model. They differ in the random-number stream and in the
carryover rule on the mean. At 0.1 week the carryover rule leaves an
off-drug drug-response mean below 0.011 points under either rule, so
it cannot account for a difference of this size. We therefore reran
the original code at 0.1 week with 4,000 new replicates (16 seeds not
used before). Power was
`r sprintf('%.3f', m6_p)` (MCSE `r sprintf('%.4f', m6_se)`), within
`r sprintf('%.1f', abs(m6_p - 0.080) / sqrt(m6_se^2 + 0.080 * 0.920 / 500))`
combined Monte Carlo SE of the reconstruction. Rerunning the stored
cell with its original seed reproduces 0.126 exactly. The rerun is
therefore consistent with the reconstruction, and the value of 0.126
is consistent with a high draw of a 500-replicate run. We found no
difference between the two implementations that would explain it.

With a constant correlation, the biomarker moderates the on-drug and
off-drug responses equally. No interaction remains to detect. The loss
of power under small carryover is therefore a property of the
correlation rule, not of carryover or of the designs.

```{r closedform}
cfv <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                          'carryover-closed-form', 'e9-closed-form-vs-mc.csv'))
cfv <- cfv[cfv$design == 'Hybrid' & cfv$construct == 'CS' & cfv$c.bm == 0.25, ]
cf_th <- c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2)
cfv_shown <- cfv[cfv$rule %in% c('step', 'graded') & cfv$t_half %in% cf_th, ]
stopifnot(nrow(cfv_shown) == 24)
cf_row <- function(rule, v) {
  sapply(cf_th, function(h) {
    x <- cfv$power[cfv$rule == rule & cfv$variant == v & cfv$t_half == h]
    stopifnot(length(x) == 1)
    x
  })
}
tab <- data.frame(
  Rule = c('Constant (original)', '', 'Decaying', ''),
  Statistic = rep(c('E9', 'E9b'), 2),
  rbind(cf_row('step', 'E9'), cf_row('step', 'E9b'),
        cf_row('graded', 'E9'), cf_row('graded', 'E9b')))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
  col.names = c('Correlation rule', 'Statistic', '0', '0.1', '0.2', '0.5', '1', '2'),
  caption = paste0('Closed-form power by carryover half-life (weeks). Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, compound symmetry. Constant: the original rule (constant correlation after first exposure). Decaying: the extended rule (correlation decaying at the carryover half-life). E9: paired-difference statistic on post-baseline visits; E9b: the same with baseline counted as an off-drug visit, as in the original analysis. Against Monte Carlo estimates (5,000 replicates per cell), ', sum(abs(cfv_shown$power_z) > 2), ' of the ', nrow(cfv_shown), ' cell-variants in this table differ by more than 2 Monte Carlo SE, and ', cf_beyond, ' of all ', cf_n, ' cell-variants of study 1 (about ', cf_expect, ' expected by chance).'))
```

```{r powerfig, fig.cap = 'Closed-form power (lines) against carryover half-life, with Monte Carlo estimates (points; 5,000 replicates per cell), under the original rule (constant correlation after first exposure) and the extended rule (correlation decaying at the carryover half-life). Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, compound symmetry; left panel E9b, right panel E9.', out.width = '85%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../../docs/figures/37-fig1-power-closed-form-cov.png')
```

We extended the DGP so the correlation decays after discontinuation at
the carryover half-life: $g_t = 1$ on drug, $2^{-t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}}$
off drug after exposure, and 0 before any exposure. This is the
pharmacological reading of a predictive biomarker. The biomarker
predicts the size of the drug effect, so it cannot predict a drug
effect that is no longer present. Under the extended rule the mean of
$g_t$ over the off-drug visits is

$$
\bar g_{\text{off}}(t_{1/2}) = \frac{1}{n_{\text{off}}}
  \sum_{t\,\text{off}} 2^{-t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}},
$$

which is strictly increasing in $t_{1/2}$, because every off-drug visit
has $t_{sd} \ge 1$ week. Two consequences follow.

- **Power is strictly decreasing in the half-life** for the
  path-stratified paired-difference statistic. This holds on every
  path with at least one off-drug visit after an exposure (Proposition
  3, Appendix A.3). The placebo-first crossover path, whose off-drug
  visits all precede exposure, has constant power. For the pooled
  statistic power is non-increasing at every step of a 120-point grid
  from 0.03 to 4 weeks. For the original mixed model it was checked
  only at the simulated half-lives.
- **The loss vanishes faster than any power of the half-life as
  $t_{1/2} \to 0$.** At 0.1 week, $\bar g_{\text{off}} \le 2^{-10}$
  and power is unchanged to within 0.001.

The original rule is the limit of the extended rule as
$t_{1/2} \to \infty$, applied at every positive half-life.

Power depends on the correlation profile only through the on/off
correlation difference $\mathcal G = 1 - \bar g_{\text{off}}$ (Figure
\@ref(fig:gapfig)). The difference is 1 without carryover. Under the
extended rule in the Hybrid design it is 0.9997 at 0.1 week, 0.991 at
0.2, 0.906 at 0.5, 0.754 at 1 and 0.551 at 2. Under the original rule
it is 0 at every positive half-life. The noncentrality is proportional
to $r_{\Delta B}/\sqrt{1 - r_{\Delta B}^2}$, and $r_{\Delta B}$ is
proportional to the difference. For small $r_{\Delta B}$ the sample
size needed for a given power therefore scales approximately as
$1/\mathcal G^2$. At 1 week this is about 1.8 times the no-carryover
sample. At 2 weeks it is about 3.3 times.

```{r gapfig, fig.cap = 'Closed-form power against the on/off correlation difference, with the positions of the two correlation rules. Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, E9.', out.width = '75%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../../docs/figures/37-fig2-power-vs-gap-cov.png')
```

Replacing only the correlation lines of the original code with the
extended rule (Appendix B.1) and running the pipeline unchanged gave
the results in Table \@ref(tab:patch). The two versions coincide
without carryover, as they must. At the original half-lives the
extended version keeps the full interaction, within Monte Carlo error
of the no-carryover value of 0.668. At 1 week it shows a gradual
decline. No matrix was repaired in either version, because
$c_{bm} = 0.25$ is below the feasibility bound.

```{r patch}
gp <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                         'hendrickson-problems', 'graded-patch',
                         'graded-patch-reps500.csv'))
stopifnot(all(gp$reps == 500), all(gp$repairs == 0))
gp_pub <- gp[gp$version == 'published', ][order(gp$t_half[gp$version == 'published']), ]
gp_gr <- gp[gp$version == 'graded', ][order(gp$t_half[gp$version == 'graded']), ]
stopifnot(identical(gp_pub$t_half, gp_gr$t_half))
tab <- data.frame(th = as.character(gp_pub$t_half),
  pm = gp_pub$mean_beta, gm = gp_gr$mean_beta,
  pp = gp_pub$power, gp = gp_gr$power)
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
  col.names = c('$t_{1/2}$ (weeks)', 'Mean estimate, original', 'Mean estimate, decaying',
                'Power, original', 'Power, decaying'), escape = FALSE,
  caption = paste0('The original code at commit 58b32a9, as published (original) and with the decaying correlation (decaying): Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, 500 replicates per cell, same seeds. Monte Carlo SE of power at most 0.022. ', sprintf('A rerun of the original version at 0.1 week with 4,000 new replicates gave power %.3f (Stage 2 text).', m6_p)))
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc) repeats Figure 4B of the original study on
the original code, for all four designs, both sample sizes and the
five censoring patterns, as published and with the decaying
correlation. It uses $c_{bm} = 0.25$ instead of the original 0.6. The
value 0.6 lies above every feasibility bound in this paper and would
confound the comparison with the repair. At 0.25 neither version
repaired a matrix, so the correlation rule is the only difference.
With 250 replicates per cell the Monte Carlo SE reaches 0.032, so a
difference of 0.05 between adjacent cells is within Monte Carlo error.
Only the pattern across cells should be read. Results at $N = 70$
without censoring:

- **Hybrid design.** Power under the original rule falls from 0.66 to
  0.08 at both positive half-lives. Power under the extended rule
  stays at 0.62 and 0.68.
- **Open label plus blinded discontinuation.** Power under the
  original rule falls from 0.57 to 0.12 and 0.13. Power under the
  extended rule stays at 0.57 and 0.60.
- **Crossover.** Power under the original rule falls only to 0.34 and
  0.33. The placebo-first path's off-drug visits precede any exposure
  and so keep zero correlation under both rules. Power under the
  extended rule stays at 0.71 and 0.78.
- **Open label.** There are no off-drug visits. The two rules coincide
  and power is low throughout.

The same pattern holds at $N = 35$ and under every censoring pattern.

```{r fig4bmc, fig.cap = 'Power to detect the biomarker-by-treatment interaction, in the layout of Figure 4B of the original study, from the original code at commit 58b32a9 as published (upper two panel rows) and with the decaying correlation (lower two panel rows). Rows within panels: censoring patterns; columns: carryover half-life; panels: trial design (N-of-1 is the Hybrid design) and total sample size. $c_{bm} = 0.25$, 250 replicates per cell (Monte Carlo SE at most 0.032), the same seeds for both versions. No matrix was repaired in either version.', out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../figures/quick-sim/hendrickson-problems/fig4b-graded-cbm0.25.png')
```

```{r fig4bg10data}
## G10 and G9 under the original parameters: driver 19 with
## --params published (referee report 2026-11-01, M1). The stored
## g10-planning/ and g9-planning/ runs used other response SDs and are
## not read. Until the published-set output is in place, every number
## that depends on it prints as [pending].
pub_dir <- file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                     'carryover-closed-form', 'published-planning')
pub_ok <- function(f, dir = pub_dir) {
  p <- file.path(dir, f)
  m <- file.path(dir, 'PARAM_SET')
  if (file.exists(p) && file.exists(m) &&
      identical(readLines(m, n = 1L), 'published')) p else NA_character_
}
PENDING <- '\\textbf{[pending]}'
pend <- function(have, expr) if (have) expr else PENDING
## Two rates differ when they are more than two combined Monte Carlo
## SEs apart.
rate_cmp <- function(p1, n1, p0, n0) {
  se <- sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n1 + p0 * (1 - p0) / n0)
  if (abs(p1 - p0) <= 2 * se) 0L else as.integer(sign(p1 - p0))
}

f4_file <- pub_ok('fig4b-g10-cbm0.25.csv')
have_f4 <- !is.na(f4_file)
if (have_f4) g9f <- read.csv(f4_file)
f4_row <- function(d, N, th, cens = 'No censoring')
  g9f[g9f$design == d & g9f$N == N & g9f$t_half == th &
      g9f$censoring == cens, ]
g9f_pick <- function(d, N, th, cens = 'No censoring') pend(have_f4, {
  r <- f4_row(d, N, th, cens)
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1)
  sprintf('%.2f', r$power)
})
g9f_mcse_max <- pend(have_f4, sprintf('%.3f',
  max(sqrt(g9f$power * (1 - g9f$power) / g9f$n_conv), na.rm = TRUE)))
## Power at 0.1 and 0.2 week against the no-carryover value, N = 70,
## no censoring.
f4_cmp <- function(d) pend(have_f4, {
  r0 <- f4_row(d, 70, 0)
  s <- vapply(c(0.1, 0.2), function(th) {
    r1 <- f4_row(d, 70, th)
    k <- rate_cmp(r1$power, r1$n_conv, r0$power, r0$n_conv)
    if (k == 0L) 'within Monte Carlo error of it' else
      sprintf('%s, at %.2f', if (k < 0L) 'lower' else 'higher', r1$power)
  }, '')
  if (s[1] == s[2]) paste(s[1], 'at both half-lives') else
    sprintf('%s at 0.1 week and %s at 0.2 week', s[1], s[2])
})
## The censoring pattern with the lowest power, Hybrid, N = 70, 0.2 week.
f4_low <- if (have_f4) {
  r <- g9f[g9f$design == 'N-of-1' & g9f$N == 70 & g9f$t_half == 0.2 &
           g9f$censoring != 'No censoring', ]
  r[which.min(r$power), ]
} else NULL
f4_low_name <- pend(have_f4, sprintf("the '%s' pattern", f4_low$censoring))
f4_low_pow <- pend(have_f4, sprintf('%.2f', f4_low$power))
## Crossover under G10 against the original code with the decaying
## correlation (lower panels of the preceding figure), N = 70, no
## censoring, at 0, 0.1 and 0.2 week.
orig_f4 <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                              'hendrickson-problems', 'fig4b-graded',
                              'fig4b-graded-cbm0.25-reps250.csv'))
f4_co_k <- if (have_f4) vapply(c(0, 0.1, 0.2), function(th) {
  g <- f4_row('CO', 70, th)
  o <- orig_f4[orig_f4$version == 'graded' & orig_f4$design == 'CO' &
               orig_f4$N == 70 & orig_f4$t_half == th &
               orig_f4$censoring == 'No censoring', ]
  stopifnot(nrow(g) == 1, nrow(o) == 1)
  rate_cmp(g$power, g$n_conv, o$power, o$n)
}, 0L) else NULL
## Completes 'In the crossover design, G10 power is ... the original
## analysis on the original code'.
f4_co_txt <- pend(have_f4, {
  if (all(f4_co_k < 0)) 'below that of' else
  if (all(f4_co_k > 0)) 'above that of' else
  if (all(f4_co_k == 0)) 'within Monte Carlo error of that of' else
    sprintf('different, at %d of the three half-lives, from that of',
            sum(f4_co_k != 0))
})
f4_co_lower <- have_f4 && all(f4_co_k < 0)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bg10) repeats the grid of Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc)
under the extended DGP of Stage 7 with the analysis G10 that the
companion paper recommends [@pmsimstats-paper02]. G10 is a
random-intercept model with CAR(1) residual correlation and an
exposure-decayed drug indicator whose half-life is chosen by AIC on
the model without the interaction, with CR2 cluster-robust standard
errors (planning section). Both figures use the original response and
baseline parameters (Methods). The data-generating process differs
from that of Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc) in its correlation structure
(separable AR(1) at $\rho = 0.7$ instead of compound symmetry) and in
its carryover rule on the mean, and the analysis differs, so the two
figures are not matched cell by cell. Each cell has 250 replicates and
a Monte Carlo SE of at most `r g9f_mcse_max`. The open-label design is not
estimable under G10: every visit is on drug, so the exposure-decayed
indicator is constant at 1 and the interaction term is collinear with
the biomarker. The original analysis replaces the interaction with a
biomarker-by-time term in that case. G10 has no such substitute, and
the cells are marked as not estimable rather than simulated. The
censoring patterns in this figure use the corrected dropout rule.
The original `censordata()` raised dropout with improvement, the
reverse of the intended mechanism, through a sign error in its biased
term (Appendix B.5). Under the corrected rule, dropout rises with
worsening. Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc) keeps the published rule, because
it reproduces the original code. Results at $N = 70$ without
censoring:

- **Hybrid design.** Power is `r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0)`,
  `r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0.1)` and `r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0.2)`
  at half-lives of 0, 0.1 and 0.2 week.
- **Open label plus blinded discontinuation.** Power is
  `r g9f_pick('OL+BDC', 70, 0)`, `r g9f_pick('OL+BDC', 70, 0.1)` and
  `r g9f_pick('OL+BDC', 70, 0.2)`.
- **Crossover.** Power is `r g9f_pick('CO', 70, 0)`,
  `r g9f_pick('CO', 70, 0.1)` and `r g9f_pick('CO', 70, 0.2)`.

Under G10 and the extended DGP, power at the pharmacological
half-lives, compared with its no-carryover value, is
`r f4_cmp('N-of-1')` in the Hybrid design, `r f4_cmp('OL+BDC')` in the
OL+BDC design and `r f4_cmp('CO')` in the crossover design. Here two
rates differ when they are more than two combined Monte Carlo SEs
apart. Of the censoring patterns, `r f4_low_name` gives the lowest
power in the Hybrid design at 0.2 week, `r f4_low_pow`. In the
crossover design, G10 power is `r f4_co_txt` the original analysis on
the original code with the decaying correlation (Figure
\@ref(fig:fig4bmc), lower two panel rows).`r if (f4_co_lower) ' The crossover design has a constant expectancy, and G10 estimates the half-life from a design with only one switch per path.' else ''`
We do not separate the contribution of the correlation structure from
that of the analysis here.

```{r fig4bg10, eval = have_f4, fig.cap = paste0('Power of the analysis G10 to detect the biomarker-by-treatment interaction under the extended DGP (separable AR(1), $\\rho = 0.7$, $c_1 = 0.2$, decaying correlation, carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean, original response parameters), in the layout of Figure 4B of the original study. Rows within panels: censoring patterns; columns: carryover half-life; panels: trial design (N-of-1 is the Hybrid design) and total sample size. $c_{bm} = 0.25$, 250 replicates per cell (Monte Carlo SE at most ', g9f_mcse_max, '). Censoring patterns use the corrected dropout rule, under which dropout rises with worsening; the original-code figure uses the published rule of commit 58b32a9. Gray cells (n/e): the open-label design, in which every visit is on drug and the interaction is not estimable under G10.'), out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.2}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(fd, aes(factor(t_half), censoring, fill = power)) +
  geom_tile(color = 'white') +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 2.8) +
  facet_grid(N ~ design) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = 'RdYlBu', limits = c(0, 1),
