Figure \@ref(fig:fig4b) extends the comparison over interaction
strengths and longer half-lives. It shows closed-form power in the
Hybrid design for each correlation rule.

- **The original rule.** Every column after $t_{1/2} = 0$ falls to the
  test size or just above it, at every strength. For example, at
  $c_{bm} = 0.2$ power under E9b falls from 0.46 to 0.07.
- **The extended rule.** Power declines smoothly: 0.46, 0.46, 0.46,
  0.41, 0.32 and 0.23 at the same strength over half-lives of 0 to 2
  weeks.
- **Feasibility.** Gray cells mark effect sizes at or above the
  compound-symmetry feasibility bound, where no joint distribution
  exists. Under the extended rule, $c_{bm} = 0.3$ becomes feasible
  only from $t_{1/2} = 1$ week. A correlation that decays instead of
  switching places a smaller demand on the structure (Appendix A.5).

```{r fig4b, fig.cap = 'Closed-form power of the paired-difference statistic by interaction strength ($c_{bm}$) and carryover half-life, in the layout of Figure 4B of the original study: the original rule and the decaying correlation. Upper row: E9b, which counts baseline as an off-drug visit as the original analysis does; lower row: E9. Gray cells: $c_{bm}$ at or above the compound-symmetry feasibility bound, where the correlation matrix is not positive definite. Hybrid design, $N = 70$, compound symmetry.', out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../../docs/figures/37-fig3-power-heatmap-cov.png')
```

The extended DGP uses the decaying correlation. The choice rests on
identifiability under carryover and on fidelity to the pharmacology.
Two limitations of the choice are stated here. First, at the
pharmacological half-lives of 0.1 to 0.2 week the on/off correlation
difference is within 0.01 of 1. The extension therefore returns the
no-carryover result. The extended DGP at its default half-life is not
a test bed for carryover. The smooth decline is a statement about
half-lives of 0.5 week and above, which we label behavioral. Second,
the decaying correlation is asymmetric. Off drug the moderation fades
with the drug effect. On drug it is the full $c_{bm}\sigma_{BR}b_i$ at
every visit, including the first weeks of titration when the Gompertz
mean is a small fraction of its maximum. A correlation proportional to
the current drug-response mean at every visit, or a correlation
half-life separate from the mean's, would remove the asymmetry.
Neither was tried. The sensitivity model of the Discussion is the form
that addresses it. The mixed-model power of the extended DGP at
half-lives of 0.5 to 2 weeks, with the half-life fixed in the analysis
or chosen from the data, is the subject of a companion paper
[@pmsimstats-paper02].

## Stage 3. Carryover on the mean

The original carryover rule decays the previous visit's mean by the
total time since discontinuation. At the second and later off-drug
visits that mean has already been decayed, so the decay compounds.
Consider two off-drug visits at weeks 11 and 12 following
discontinuation at week 10. The original code decays the week-10 value
by $2^{-1/t_{1/2}}$ and then by $2^{-2/t_{1/2}}$, a total exponent of
3 weeks for 2 weeks elapsed. Whether this was intended is not stated
in the original study, and we do not claim that it was not. We treat
the two forms as two specifications.

The extended DGP decays the mean from the last on-drug value,
$\mu_{BR,\text{last}}\,2^{-t_{sd}/t_{1/2}}$. The mean at any off-drug
visit then depends only on the elapsed time (Appendix B.3).

The choice changes no slope, variance or feasibility bound. It changes
only the path means. It therefore changes the closed-form power of
study 1 by at most 0.002 in the Hybrid design. In the original
pipeline it changes power by at most 0.006. Figure \@ref(fig:trajfig)
shows the drug-response mean by visit for the four Hybrid paths under
both forms. Two features are visible. At $t_{1/2} = 1$ week the
original rule lies below the extended rule at the second off-drug
visit, as expected. At 0.2 week both are indistinguishable from zero
one week after discontinuation. At re-exposure (week 16 in paths 1 and
3) time on drug restarts at zero. The mean then rises along a fresh
Gompertz curve to 4.3 points at the week-16 visit, four weeks into the
restarted curve. The residual from the earlier exposure has decayed to
0.16 points by then even at a 1-week half-life. No downward step
therefore appears on the Hybrid schedule. A step would appear only if
a visit fell within about a week of re-exposure at a half-life of a
week or more.

```{r trajfig, fig.cap = 'Drug-response mean by visit in the Hybrid design, by path, under the extended carryover rule (decay from the last on-drug mean, the extended DGP) and the original carryover rule (compounded decay), at carryover half-lives of 0.2 and 1 week. Filled points: on-drug visits; open points: off-drug visits. D: drug; P: placebo.', out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../../docs/figures/01-fig-hybrid-br-mean-reexposure.png')
```

The extended DGP decays carryover from the last on-drug mean. It keeps
the original restart of time on drug at re-exposure, which for
prazosin matches re-titration after an interruption. For drugs without
titration the response should instead rebuild from its residual level.
That is an option, not the default. The choice rests on fidelity to
the pharmacology, as a judgment. The numerical consequence is at most
0.006 in power either way.

## Stage 4. Serial correlation

The original DGP uses compound symmetry. Visits one week apart and
sixteen weeks apart have the same correlation of 0.8. We have no PTSD
symptom series with which to decide whether that overstates long-lag
correlation, and we do not claim that it does. Both compound symmetry
and AR(1) are used in N-of-1 simulation [@chen2014]. Serial
correlation has been discussed as a design consideration for
personalized studies [@schork2022]. Two elements are open: the form of
the within-component correlation, and its value.

The extended DGP uses AR(1) in calendar weeks,
$\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$, with one $\rho$ for all three
components. The value of $\rho$ is a parameter. We take $\rho = 0.7$
as a convention only, not an estimate. Under the adopted separable
form the original effect size of 0.3 is already feasible at
$\rho = 0.8$ (bound 0.440), so feasibility at 0.3 does not determine
the value. Of the four values in Table \@ref(tab:rhostage), 0.7 has
the largest separable feasibility bound (0.474). The value should be
read with the sensitivity range of that table.

Table \@ref(tab:rhostage) shows what $\rho$ does under compound
symmetry and under the structure adopted in Stage 5, for
$\rho \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$. Under compound symmetry alone,
lowering $\rho_{cs}$ from 0.8 to 0.7 raises the feasibility bound from
0.256 to 0.346. The original effect size of 0.3 then becomes feasible
by the change of $\rho$ alone, with no change of structure. The same
change lowers closed-form power at $c_{bm} = 0.25$ from 0.721 to
0.628. A lower serial correlation leaves more within-person noise in
the on-minus-off contrast. The two criteria pull in opposite
directions. The feasible range widens as $\rho$ falls, and the power
at a matched $c_{bm}$ falls.

```{r rhostage}
rs_dir <- file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim', 'carryover-closed-form',
                    'rho-stage')
rs_ceil <- read.csv(file.path(rs_dir, 'ceilings-by-rho-min.csv'))
rs_pow <- read.csv(file.path(rs_dir, 'power-by-rho.csv'))
rs_rho <- c(0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8)
rs_get <- function(d, con, th, col, v = NULL) {
  sapply(rs_rho, function(r) {
    k <- d$rho == r & d$construct == con & d$t_half == th
    if (!is.null(v)) k <- k & d$variant == v
    stopifnot(sum(k) == 1)
    d[[col]][k]
  })
}
tab <- data.frame(
  rho = as.character(rs_rho),
  cs_ceil = rs_get(rs_ceil, 'CS', 0, 'min_ceiling'),
  cs_pow = rs_get(rs_pow, 'CS', 0, 'power', 'E9'),
  sep_ceil = rs_get(rs_ceil, 'sep', 0, 'min_ceiling'),
  sep_pow = rs_get(rs_pow, 'sep', 0, 'power', 'E9'))
rs_drop <- c(tab$cs_pow - rs_get(rs_pow, 'CS', 0.2, 'power', 'E9'),
             tab$sep_pow - rs_get(rs_pow, 'sep', 0.2, 'power', 'E9'))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
  col.names = c('$\\rho_{cs}$ or $\\rho$', 'Ceiling', 'Power at $c_{bm} = 0.25$',
                'Ceiling', 'Power at $c_{bm} = 0.25$'), escape = FALSE,
  caption = paste0('Serial correlation: the feasibility bound on $c_{bm}$ (Ceiling; decaying correlation, no carryover, minimum over the Hybrid, crossover and OL+BDC designs) and closed-form E9 power (Hybrid, $N = 70$, no carryover) by $\\rho$, under compound symmetry and under the separable AR(1) form of Stage 5. Under compound symmetry the Hybrid and crossover designs tie for the minimum. Under the separable form the minimum is attained in the Hybrid design at $\\rho = 0.8$ and in the OL+BDC design at $\\rho \\le 0.7$, and the crossover design is never binding. ',
                   sprintf('At $t_{1/2} = 0.2$ week every power value is lower by %.3f to %.3f.',
                           min(rs_drop), max(rs_drop)))) |>
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(' ' = 1, 'Compound symmetry' = 2, 'Separable AR(1)' = 2))
```

The extended DGP uses AR(1) in weeks at $\rho = 0.7$. The choice rests
on existence, traded against power. The calibration status is open.
The AR(1) form is adopted for the reason given in Stage 5 (it is what
the analysis model assumes), not because compound symmetry has been
shown wrong for these data. Any study using the DGP should report
$\rho$. Where the conclusion could depend on it, the analysis should be
repeated at 0.6 and 0.8.

## Stage 5. Cross-component structure

The original DGP has a same-visit cross-component correlation
$c_1 = 0.2$ and an other-visit correlation $c_\times = 0.1$ at every
lag. With AR(1) within components, the direct translation keeps $c_1$
at lag zero and lets the other-visit correlation decay,
$c_\times\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$. This two-constant form is what
the package's `buildSigma()` builds when its two constants differ
(Appendix B.5). It is not the only choice, and it has a validity
condition.

The extended DGP uses the separable form,
$c_1\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$ at every lag including zero. The
response block is then a Kronecker product $M = K \otimes A$ of a
$3 \times 3$ component correlation $K$ (1 on the diagonal, $c_1$ off
it) and one AR(1) kernel $A_{ts} = \rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$. In
words, every component has the same first-order autoregressive
correlation, and the between-component correlation is constant at
every lag. It is the two-constant form with $c_\times = c_1$. The
original same-visit value $c_1 = 0.2$ is kept. Four properties follow
(Appendix A.5).

1. **Validity for every schedule.** The eigenvalues of $M$ are products
   of those of $K$ and $A$, so $M$ is positive definite for any visit
   times. The two-constant form adds a same-visit cross-component term
   that carries correlation without variance. It is positive definite
   only when the smallest eigenvalue of $A$ exceeds
   $(c_1 - c_\times)/(1 - c_\times) = 0.111$. On the paper's schedules
   the condition holds (smallest eigenvalue 0.122 in the Hybrid and
   OL+BDC designs at $\rho = 0.8$, 0.193 at 0.7; 0.28 and 0.43 in the
   crossover design). On 20 weekly visits at $\rho = 0.8$ it holds by
   less than 0.001. On daily measurement over eight weeks it fails
   (0.016 at $\rho = 0.8$, 0.026 at 0.7). The two-constant form
   therefore cannot be used for the dense schedules that wearable or
   diary outcomes produce.
2. **The original structure is already of this kind in pieces.** It is
   the sum of a person-level and an occasion-level separable term,
   each valid. This is why the original matrices fail only through the
   biomarker row, never in the response block.
3. **An exact, interpretable feasibility bound.** The bound factors
   into a component term and a schedule term,
   $$
   c_{bm}^{*} = \sqrt{1 - R^2}\;\bigl(g^\top A^{-1} g\bigr)^{-1/2},
   \qquad R^2 = \frac{2c_1^2}{1 + c_1},
   $$
   where $R^2$ is the squared multiple correlation of the drug response
   on the other two components at one visit. The schedule term is a
   sum of per-step terms of the correlation profile. A profile that
   switches abruptly between closely spaced visits has a large
   per-step term. This is why designs with many on-off switches can
   carry only small effects.
4. **It nearly matches the analysis model.** Under separability the
   summed response has covariance $(s_t^\top K s_s)\,\rho^{\lvert w_t
   - w_s\rvert}$, with $s_t$ the component SDs at visit $t$ (Appendix
   A.5). With constant SDs this is exactly AR(1), the residual
   structure `corCAR1` assumes. In the Hybrid design the
   placebo-response SD is $10\eta_t$, so it halves at blinding. The
   summed-response variance is then 368 at open-label visits and 257
   at blinded visits. The correlation between an open-label and a
   blinded visit is the AR(1) value times 0.976. The summed response is
   therefore AR(1) only within a phase. Under the two-constant form it
   is, in addition, AR(1) plus a white-noise term the analysis model
   omits. These statements follow from the algebra. Their effect on
   test calibration has not been measured separately.

Table \@ref(tab:ceilings) gives the feasibility bounds. At the
original $\rho = 0.8$ the two-constant form raises the bound only to
0.291. A single same-visit correlation repeated across visits that
share little demands more of the biomarker row. In the open-label
design, where every visit is on drug, it lowers the bound. The
separable form raises the bound to 0.440. At $\rho = 0.7$ the two
forms are close, 0.452 against 0.474. At the recommended $\rho$ the
separable form's gain in feasible range is therefore small, and its
reasons are properties 1 and 4. The bound of 0.474 is attained in the
OL+BDC design (0.480 in the Hybrid design). A correlation of 0.45 is
feasible in every design without carryover. Effects as large as the
original 0.6 exceed every feasibility bound in the Hybrid design.

The wider feasible range has a consequence that does not depend on
the form. At the same $c_{bm}$, AR(1) data carry less information
about the interaction than compound-symmetric data. The closed-form
power of the paired-difference statistic in the Hybrid design at
$c_{bm} = 0.25$ falls from 0.721 under the original structure to 0.335
under the separable form at $\rho = 0.8$ and 0.290 at $\rho = 0.7$. A
larger feasible correlation does not by itself mean more power. Effect
sizes under different structures should therefore be compared on the
scale of the implied slope, not of $c_{bm}$.

```{r ceilings}
cl_ceil <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                              'carryover-closed-form', 'rho-stage',
                              'ceilings-by-rho-min.csv'))
cl_get <- function(r, con) {
  x <- cl_ceil$min_ceiling[cl_ceil$rho == r & cl_ceil$construct == con &
                           cl_ceil$t_half == 0]
  stopifnot(length(x) == 1)
  x
}
tab <- data.frame(rho = c('0.8', '0.7'),
                  cs = c(cl_get(0.8, 'CS'), cl_get(0.7, 'CS')),
                  f = c(cl_get(0.8, 'two'), cl_get(0.7, 'two')),
                  c = c(cl_get(0.8, 'sep'), cl_get(0.7, 'sep')))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
  col.names = c('$\\rho_{cs}$ or $\\rho$', 'Compound symmetry', 'AR(1), two-constant cross-component', 'Separable AR(1)'),
  escape = FALSE,
  caption = 'Largest feasible biomarker-response correlation $c_{bm}$ under the decaying correlation, without carryover, minimum over the Hybrid, crossover and OL+BDC designs. Under compound symmetry the Hybrid and crossover designs tie for the minimum. Under the two AR(1) forms the minimum is attained in the Hybrid design at $\\rho = 0.8$ and in the OL+BDC design at $\\rho = 0.7$ (separable form: Hybrid 0.480), and the crossover design is never binding.')
```

The extended DGP uses the separable form with $c_1 = 0.2$. The choice
rests on analyzability (property 4) and existence (properties 1 and
3). The value $c_1 = 0.2$ is the original value and is uncalibrated.

## Stage 6. Features the extended DGP adds

The original DGP correlates the biomarker with the drug response only.
A biomarker that is also prognostic, through an association with the
natural history, the placebo response or baseline severity, cannot be
represented. A simulation built on the original DGP therefore cannot
show whether an analysis stays valid under such a biomarker.

The extended DGP adds optional correlations of the biomarker with the
natural-history component or the placebo-response component (constant
over visits, or growing along the natural-history curve) and with
baseline severity. It adds phase-specific measurement error, a Weibull
decay form and monotone dropout as further options.

**A prognostic biomarker.** We simulated a correlation of 0.3 between
the biomarker and the natural-history component (constant, or growing
along its curve), the placebo-response component, or baseline
severity, with no interaction. Analyses that keep baseline as an
outcome row use one biomarker main effect $\beta_B$ for baseline and
for the off-drug visits. When the biomarker is prognostic through a
pathway that is absent at baseline, those two associations differ.
Part of the difference is attributed to the interaction (Appendix
A.4). Every analysis that shares the biomarker effect with baseline
exceeded the nominal level in at least one such cell (Table
\@ref(tab:prognostic)).

```{r stressdata}
ss_dir <- file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim', 'carryover-closed-form',
                    'strawman-stress')
## Main run plus the two post hoc files fitted to the same trials; S is
## refitted in each post hoc file as a pairing check and dropped there.
ss_read <- function(tag) {
  x <- lapply(c('summary-full', 'summary-full-extra', 'summary-full-extra2'),
              function(b) {
    d <- read.csv(file.path(ss_dir, paste0(b, tag, '.csv')))
    if (b != 'summary-full') d <- d[d$analysis != 'S', ]
    d[, c('label', 'cbm', 'analysis', 'reject', 'fits')]
  })
  do.call(rbind, x)
}
ss2 <- ss_read('-anchored')
ss1 <- ss_read('')
ss_r <- function(d, lab, an, cbm = 0) {
  v <- d$reject[d$label == lab & d$cbm == cbm & d$analysis == an]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
ss_f <- function(v) sprintf('%.3f', v)
ss_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) return(paste(x, collapse = ''))
  paste0(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ', '), ' and ', x[length(x)])
}
ss_an <- c(
  R = 'Original analysis (random intercept, model-based)',
  S = 'Random intercept + CAR(1), CR2',
  DS = 'The same, half-life chosen by AIC',
  A = 'Unstructured covariance, Kenward-Roger',
  DA = 'The same, half-life chosen by AIC',
  F1 = 'Random intercept + CAR(1) with expectancy terms, CR2',
  G1 = 'The same, with phase-specific residual variances, CR2',
  G2 = 'The same, with phase-specific residual variances, model-based',
  F1A = 'Expectancy terms, half-life chosen by AIC, CR2',
  ES = 'Random intercept + CAR(1) with free baseline slope, CR2')
ss_short <- c(R = 'the original analysis', S = 'the CAR(1) model with CR2',
              DS = 'the CAR(1) model with AIC-chosen half-life',
              A = 'the unstructured model',
              DA = 'the unstructured model with AIC-chosen half-life',
              F1 = 'the expectancy-term model',
              G1 = 'the expectancy-term model with phase-specific variances (CR2)',
              G2 = 'the expectancy-term model with phase-specific variances (model-based)',
              F1A = 'the expectancy-term model with AIC-chosen half-life',
              ES = 'the free-baseline model')
ss_prog <- c('prog-TV-const', 'prog-TV-grow', 'prog-PB', 'prog-BL')
ss_cell <- c(`prog-TV-const` = 'the constant natural-history pathway',
             `prog-TV-grow` = 'the growing natural-history pathway',
             `prog-PB` = 'the placebo pathway',
             `prog-BL` = 'the baseline-severity pathway',
             `curve-C07` = 'the base cell', `curve-CS` = 'compound symmetry',
             `meas-error` = 'measurement error', N35 = '$N = 35$',
             N150 = '$N = 150$', thalf0 = '$t_{1/2} = 0$',
             thalf1 = '$t_{1/2} = 1$ week',
             weibull0.5 = 'Weibull decay with shape 0.5',
             weibull2 = 'Weibull decay with shape 2',
             `dropout-MCAR` = 'dropout completely at random',
             `dropout-MAR` = 'dropout dependent on the last score')
ss_tab <- function(d) {
  sapply(ss_prog, function(l) sapply(names(ss_an), function(a) ss_r(d, l, a)))
}
ss_m2 <- ss_tab(ss2)
ss_m1 <- ss_tab(ss1)
ss_bold <- function(m) {
  matrix(ifelse(m > 0.075, sprintf('\\textbf{%.3f}', m), sprintf('%.3f', m)),
         nrow(m), dimnames = dimnames(m))
}
ss_band1 <- 0.05 + c(-2, 2) * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 1000)
## Cells whose classification changed between the runs, against the
## bold threshold (0.075) and against the single-cell band.
ss_cross <- function(thr) {
  k <- which((ss_m1 > thr) != (ss_m2 > thr), arr.ind = TRUE)
  if (!nrow(k)) return('none')
  paste(sprintf('%s under %s (%s to %s)',
                ss_short[rownames(ss_m2)[k[, 1]]],
                ss_cell[colnames(ss_m2)[k[, 2]]],
                ss_f(ss_m1[k]), ss_f(ss_m2[k])), collapse = '; ')
}
ss_dmax <- max(abs(ss_m2 - ss_m1))
ss_dk <- which(abs(ss_m2 - ss_m1) == ss_dmax, arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
## Pooled size over the 11 non-prognostic null cells.
ss_np <- c('curve-C07', 'curve-CS', 'meas-error', 'N35', 'N150', 'thalf0',
           'thalf1', 'weibull0.5', 'weibull2', 'dropout-MCAR', 'dropout-MAR')
ss_pool <- function(d, an) {
  x <- d[d$cbm == 0 & d$label %in% ss_np & d$analysis == an, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) == 11)
  sum(x$reject * x$fits) / sum(x$fits)
}
ss_cmax <- function(d, an) {
  x <- d[d$cbm == 0 & d$label %in% ss_np & d$analysis == an, ]
  x[which.max(x$reject), ]
}
ss_band11 <- 2 * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 11000)
ss_fixed <- c('S', 'C1', 'F1', 'ES', 'F2', 'G1')
ss_fixed_pool <- sapply(ss_fixed, function(a) ss_pool(ss2, a))
ss_fixed_max <- max(sapply(ss_fixed, function(a) ss_cmax(ss2, a)$reject))
ss_all <- c('R', 'S', 'C1', 'C2', 'DS', 'A', 'DA', 'F1', 'F2', 'ES', 'EA',
            'G1', 'G2', 'F1A')
ss_above <- ss_all[sapply(ss_all, function(a) ss_pool(ss2, a)) > 0.05 + ss_band11]
stopifnot(all(c(ss_m2['F1', ], ss_m2['G1', ], ss_m2['G2', ], ss_m2['F1A', ]) <
              ss_band1[2]))
```

```{r prognostic}
tab <- data.frame(Analysis = unname(ss_an), ss_bold(ss_m2), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
  linesep = '',
  col.names = c('Analysis', 'Natural history, constant', 'Natural history, growing',
                'Placebo response', 'Baseline severity'),
  caption = 'Null rejection rates under a prognostic biomarker (prognostic correlation 0.3, $c_{bm} = 0$), 1,000 replicates per cell (two-MCSE band 0.036 to 0.064 for a single cell). Second run of study 3: carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean (the extended DGP) and randomized path allocation. Rates above 0.075 in bold. The first run is in Table \\@ref(tab:prognosticfirst); the per-cell changes are given in the text.') |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 9) |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = '5.5cm') |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(2:5, width = '2.1cm')
```

The expectancy-term family kept the nominal level in every prognostic
cell. Its four analyses rejected
`r ss_f(min(ss_m2[c('F1', 'G1', 'G2', 'F1A'), ]))` to
`r ss_f(max(ss_m2[c('F1', 'G1', 'G2', 'F1A'), ]))`. This family adds
the expectancy and a biomarker-by-expectancy term to the mean model,
with or without residual variances that differ by trial phase. The
free-baseline model adds `bmc:bl0`, which gives baseline its own
biomarker slope. It rejected `r ss_f(ss_m2['ES', 'prog-TV-grow'])`
under the growing natural-history pathway, above the single-cell band,
and `r ss_f(ss_m2['ES', 'prog-PB'])` under the placebo pathway.
Appendix A.4 explains why freeing the baseline slope alone is not
sufficient when the prognostic slope grows over time or scales with
the expectancy. A prognostic association with baseline severity alone
did less harm, because baseline severity enters every visit equally.
The original analysis rejected `r ss_f(ss_m2['R', 'prog-BL'])` there.
The scenarios in
which the pathway is absent at baseline are the ones that show the
inflation. Whether such a pathway, at a magnitude of 0.3, is realistic
for blood pressure in PTSD is not known, but a DGP that cannot
generate it cannot show the inflation.

**Changes from the first run.** The first run used the original
carryover rule and fixed allocation (Appendix C, Table
\@ref(tab:prognosticfirst)). The largest change in any cell of the
prognostic table was `r ss_f(ss_dmax)`, for
`r ss_short[rownames(ss_m2)[ss_dk[1]]]` under
`r ss_cell[colnames(ss_m2)[ss_dk[2]]]`. Treating the two runs as
independent, the difference between them in one cell has a Monte Carlo
SE of about 0.010 at a rate of 0.05. Cells that crossed the bold
threshold of 0.075: `r ss_cross(0.075)`. Cells that crossed the upper
edge of the single-cell band: `r ss_cross(ss_band1[2])`. The original
analysis under the growing pathway therefore moved from inside the band
to above it. The second run changed the carryover rule and the
allocation together. The stored outputs cannot separate the two
changes, so these differences are not attributed to either one.

**Feasibility with a prognostic correlation.** A prognostic
correlation occupies the same biomarker row of the correlation matrix
as $c_{bm}$. The two therefore share one feasibility condition.
Writing the row as a sum of fixed patterns scaled by the correlations,
the existence condition of Stage 1 becomes a quadratic form. The
largest value of one correlation given the others is the positive
root of a quadratic (Appendix A.4). Table \@ref(tab:jointceiling)
gives the bounds for the Hybrid design under the extended DGP. The
prognostic correlation of 0.3 used above lies inside the feasible
region at every $c_{bm}$ up to 0.45. At the stress test's half-life of
0.5 week, a prognostic correlation of 0.3 with $c_{bm} = 0.45$ lies
0.006 inside the boundary. A prognostic correlation of 0.6 is
infeasible with any $c_{bm}$. That is the combination the companion
study's two repaired runs had simulated (Stage 1). The correlations
with the placebo-response and the natural-history components have
identical bounds, because their patterns are the same constant on
every visit of one component. A correlation with baseline severity
has a looser bound, since baseline severity is uncorrelated with the
response components and enters only through its square. The OL+BDC
design is within 0.03 of the Hybrid values. The crossover design has
looser bounds throughout. We verified the bounds by checking that the
smallest eigenvalue of the full matrix is positive at 0.999 times each
bound and negative at 1.001 times it.

```{r jointceiling}
jc <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                         'carryover-closed-form', 'rho-stage',
                         'prognostic-joint-ceilings.csv'))
hyb <- jc[jc$design == 'Hybrid' & jc$t1half %in% c(0.2, 0.5), ]
rows <- data.frame(
  coupling = c('$c_{PB}$ or $c_{TV}$', '', '', '', '$c_{BL}$', '', '', '',
               '$c_{bm}$', '', ''),
  given = c('alone', '$c_{bm} = 0.25$', '$c_{bm} = 0.30$', '$c_{bm} = 0.45$',
            'alone', '$c_{bm} = 0.25$', '$c_{bm} = 0.30$', '$c_{bm} = 0.45$',
            'alone', '$c_{PB} = 0.3$', '$c_{PB} = 0.6$'),
  key_c = c(rep('c_pb', 4), rep('c_bl', 4), rep('c_bm', 3)),
  key_g = c('alone', 'c_bm = 0.25', 'c_bm = 0.3', 'c_bm = 0.45',
            'alone', 'c_bm = 0.25', 'c_bm = 0.3', 'c_bm = 0.45',
            'alone', 'c_pb = 0.3', 'c_pb = 0.6'))
pick <- function(th) {
  sapply(seq_len(nrow(rows)), function(i) {
    v <- hyb$ceiling[hyb$t1half == th & hyb$coupling == rows$key_c[i] &
                     hyb$given == rows$key_g[i]]
    if (length(v) != 1 || is.na(v)) 'none' else sprintf('%.3f', v)
  })
}
tab <- data.frame(rows$coupling, rows$given, pick(0.2), pick(0.5))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, linesep = '',
  col.names = c('Correlation', 'Given', '$t_{1/2} = 0.2$ week', '$t_{1/2} = 0.5$ week'),
  caption = 'Largest feasible prognostic correlation given the biomarker-response correlation, and the reverse, under the extended DGP (separable AR(1), $\\rho = 0.7$, $c_1 = 0.2$), Hybrid design, minimum over its four paths. Correlation: the quantity whose bound is given. $c_{PB}$, $c_{TV}$, $c_{BL}$: correlation of the biomarker with the placebo-response component, the natural-history component and baseline severity. None: no value is feasible.')
```

```{r optdata}
op_lab <- c('curve-C07', 'meas-error', 'dropout-MCAR', 'dropout-MAR',
            'weibull0.5', 'weibull2', 'thalf0', 'thalf1', 'N35', 'N150')
op_an <- c('R', 'S', 'F1')
op_get <- function(d, cbm) {
  sapply(op_an, function(a) sapply(op_lab, function(l) ss_r(d, l, a, cbm)))
}
op_n2 <- op_get(ss2, 0)
op_p2 <- op_get(ss2, 0.3)
op_n1 <- op_get(ss1, 0)
op_p1 <- op_get(ss1, 0.3)
## Change in power from the base cell, phrased by its sign.
op_chg <- function(lab) {
  v <- op_p2[lab, ] - op_p2['curve-C07', ]
  r <- sprintf('%.2f to %.2f', min(abs(v)), max(abs(v)))
  if (all(v < 0)) paste('lowered power by', r)
  else if (all(v >= 0)) paste('raised power by', r)
  else sprintf('changed power by %+.2f to %+.2f', min(v), max(v))
}
op_rng <- function(x) sprintf('%.2f to %.2f', min(x), max(x))
op_valid_max <- max(op_n2[, c('S', 'F1')])
op_R_max <- max(op_n2[, 'R'])
op_R_at <- ss_cell[rownames(op_n2)[which.max(op_n2[, 'R'])]]
```

**Size more generally.** We pooled the 11 non-prognostic null cells
(11,000 replicates). The nominal band is 0.05 plus or minus two Monte
Carlo SE, $2\sqrt{0.05 \times 0.95 / 11{,}000} = 0.004$, that is
`r ss_f(0.05 - ss_band11)` to `r ss_f(0.05 + ss_band11)`. The original
analysis rejected `r ss_f(ss_pool(ss2, 'R'))`, and
`r ss_f(ss_r(ss2, 'N35', 'R'))` at $N = 35$. The unstructured model
with Kenward-Roger inference [@kenward1997] rejected
`r ss_f(ss_pool(ss2, 'A'))`, with `r ss_f(ss_r(ss2, 'N35', 'A'))` at
$N = 35$. Random-intercept models with continuous-time AR(1) residuals
and CR2 cluster-robust standard errors [@bell2002; @pustejovsky2018],
at the fixed analysis half-life, rejected
`r ss_f(min(ss_fixed_pool))` to `r ss_f(max(ss_fixed_pool))`. No single
cell of these models exceeded `r ss_f(ss_fixed_max)`. With the
half-life chosen by AIC, the CAR(1) model rejected
`r ss_f(ss_pool(ss2, 'DS'))` and the expectancy-term model
`r ss_f(ss_pool(ss2, 'F1A'))`. The latter's largest single cell was
`r ss_f(ss_cmax(ss2, 'F1A')$reject)`, under
`r ss_cell[ss_cmax(ss2, 'F1A')$label]`. Of the analyses in this
paragraph, `r ss_list(ss_short[intersect(c('R', 'A', 'DS', 'F1A'), ss_above)])`
lie above the pooled band.

**The options.** Table \@ref(tab:options) shows what each optional
feature did to size and power for three analyses: the original
analysis, the random-intercept CAR(1) model with CR2, and the
expectancy-term model that the prognostic cells favor. Measurement
error (SD 3 open label, 6 blinded) `r op_chg('meas-error')`. Dropout
of 20% completely at random `r op_chg('dropout-MCAR')`. Dropout of
20% dependent on the last score `r op_chg('dropout-MAR')`. A Weibull
decay with the same half-life `r op_chg('weibull0.5')` at shape 0.5
(a steep early decay) and `r op_chg('weibull2')` at shape 2. The true
half-life itself moved power from `r op_rng(op_p2['thalf0', ])` at
zero to `r op_rng(op_p2['thalf1', ])` at one week. Halving $N$ gave
power of `r op_rng(op_p2['N35', ])`, against
`r op_rng(op_p2['curve-C07', ])` in the base cell. At $N = 150$ the
CAR(1) model reached `r sprintf('%.2f', op_p2['N150', 'S'])`. In these
null cells the CAR(1) and expectancy-term models rejected at most
`r ss_f(op_valid_max)`, against a single-cell band of
`r sprintf('%.4f', ss_band1[1])` to `r sprintf('%.4f', ss_band1[2])`.
The original analysis rejected up to `r ss_f(op_R_max)`, under
`r op_R_at`. The features change power, which the planning section
and the companion paper address.

Hybrid design, second run of study 3 (carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean, randomized allocation). Each row changes one feature of the base cell.') |>

**Power and robustness.** The expectancy-term model keeps its size
under every prognostic pathway and has lower power. In the base cell
of the second run its power was
`r ss_f(op_p2['curve-C07', 'F1'])` against
`r ss_f(op_p2['curve-C07', 'S'])` for the CAR(1) model. A further
1,500 trials per cell under the same DGP were pooled with the second
run (2,000 per cell). There, size-adjusted power was 0.431 against
0.496, about 13% less (repository `docs/47`). Under compound symmetry
at $c_{bm} = 0.25$ the order reverses. Power in the second run was
`r ss_f(ss_r(ss2, 'curve-CS', 'F1', 0.25))` against
`r ss_f(ss_r(ss2, 'curve-CS', 'S', 0.25))`, and size-adjusted power
0.510 against 0.490. A DGP paper can say which analyses are valid
under which features. The choice between power and robustness is the
trialist's. It depends on whether a prognostic pathway absent at
baseline is plausible for the biomarker in hand.

The extended DGP includes the prognostic correlations as an option for
that reason. The other three features are options whose effect on power is tabulated.
The choice rests on analyzability. Measurement error is implemented in
the stress-test driver and not yet in the package (Appendix B.5).

## Stage 7. The extended DGP

Table \@ref(tab:spec) collects the choices. Each row is marked as an
extension of the original DGP, a choice among open alternatives, an
option, or a retained element, and names the stage that justifies it.
Values not listed are the original values.

Table: (\#tab:spec) The extended data-generating process. The Default column gives the value of each element in the extended DGP; where the stress test of Stage 6 used another value it is stated. The stress test's second run also assigned participants to paths at random, a driver option outside the extended DGP (Appendix B.5).

| Element | Specification | Default | Kind | Justified in |
|------------|------------------------------|------------|--------|---------|
| Components | $Y_{it} = \mathrm{BL}_i - (TV_{it} + PB_{it} + BR_{it})$, Gompertz means as in the original DGP | original parameters (Methods): BR $m = 10.99$, $r = 0.42$, SD 8; PB and TV $m = 6.51$, $r = 0.35$, SD $10\eta_t$ and 10; $d = 5$; biomarker 124.3 (SD 15.4); baseline 83.1 (SD 18.5) | retained | Methods |
| Validity | stop if the correlation matrix is not positive definite | always | extension | Stage 1 |
| Biomarker-response correlation | $c_{bm}$ on drug; $c_{bm}2^{-t_{sd}/t_{1/2}}$ off drug after exposure; 0 before exposure | $c_{bm}$ below the feasibility bound of every design in the study | extension | Stage 2 |
| Carryover on the mean | decay from the last on-drug value, $\mu_{BR,\text{last}}\,2^{-t_{sd}/t_{1/2}}$ | $t_{1/2} = 0.1$ to 0.2 week (pharmacological, assumed); 0.5 in the stress test | choice | Stage 3 |
| Re-exposure | as in the original DGP: time on drug restarts at zero | on, for titrated drugs | retained | Stage 3 |
| Within-component correlation | AR(1) in weeks, $\rho^{\lvert w_t-w_s\rvert}$, one $\rho$ for all three components | $\rho = 0.7$ (convention; report and vary) | choice | Stage 4 |
| Cross-component correlation | separable, $c_1\rho^{\lvert w_t-w_s\rvert}$ at every lag; the Kronecker form applies to the correlation, since the PB SD scales with the expectancy | $c_1 = 0.2$ (original value) | choice | Stage 5 |
| Path allocation | fixed numbers, as in the original DGP | original values | retained | Methods |
| Prognostic correlations | correlation of the biomarker with TV or PB, or with baseline severity; or a mean shift of TV growing along its curve | off; 0.3 in the stress test; correlations must lie inside the joint bound with $c_{bm}$ (Table \@ref(tab:jointceiling)) | option | Stage 6 |
| Measurement error | independent, SD by phase | off; 3 open label, 6 blinded in the stress test | option (driver only) | Stage 6 |
| Decay form | exponential or Weibull with the same half-life | exponential | option | Stage 6 |
| Dropout | monotone, completely at random or at random given the last score | off; 20% in the stress test | option | Stage 6 |

## Using the extended DGP to plan a trial

**What $c_{bm}$ means.** Conditional on the biomarker, the correlation
encoding shifts the on-drug drug-response mean by $c_{bm}\sigma_{BR}$
per standard deviation of biomarker (Discussion). With the original
$\sigma_{BR} = 8$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$ is a slope of 2.0 symptom points
per SD of biomarker, 0.35 is 2.8 points, 0.45 is 3.6 points, and the
feasibility bound of 0.474 is 3.8 points. The biomarker's SD is 15.4
mm Hg in the original parameters, so 0.25 is 0.13 points per mm Hg.
The association first reported for prazosin is 14 points on the
Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale per 10 mm Hg [@raskind2016bp], or
21.5 points per SD of biomarker. Representing that slope under the
correlation encoding would need $\sigma_{BR} \ge 45$ at the bound.
That is larger than the SD of the symptom score itself (18.5 at
baseline in the original parameters). Under the original parameters
the bound is therefore below the reported association. The comparison
is approximate for two reasons. The observed slope is on the total
symptom change, not the drug-response component. And
$\sigma_{BR} = 8$ is the original choice, not an estimate.

That association did not replicate in our reanalysis of CSP 563
(`docs/69`). The interaction was +0.25 points per 10 mm Hg (95% CI
$-2.72$ to 3.21). With $\sigma_{BR} = 8$ and the trial's biomarker SD
of 14.2 mm Hg, this interval corresponds to $c_{bm}$ from $-0.57$ to
0.48. The values of $c_{bm}$ used in this paper, 0.25 to 0.45, imply
1.4 to 2.5 points per 10 mm Hg. They lie inside that interval. CSP 563
therefore neither supports nor excludes them, and it gives no reason
to plan for a slope above the feasibility bound. A study that does
need a larger slope should use the sensitivity model of the
Discussion once it is implemented, or raise $\sigma_{BR}$ with a
stated reason.

**What CSP 563 identifies.** The reanalysis estimates some quantities
of the DGP on the total symptom score, all as computed in `docs/69`
and not re-estimated here. The baseline SD is 16.0 (DGP: 18.5) and
the biomarker SD 14.2 mm Hg (DGP: 15.4). The biomarker is not
prognostic for baseline severity ($r = 0.02$, 95% CI $-0.09$ to
0.13), which supports a zero prognostic correlation with baseline. The
placebo-arm improvement has the DGP's time course and is about 1.8
times its size. The SD of change from baseline grows from 17 to 24
points over 26 weeks, where the DGP holds it at 16.0. The total-score
correlation decays by about 0.975 per week with about 10 percent
measurement noise. The DGP's total-score correlation falls faster at
short lags and then flattens. The trial does not identify the split
between the natural-history and placebo-response components, the
expectancy weight, the component-level correlations or the carryover
half-life. All participants were blinded throughout, and no one
stopped drug. A sensitivity arm of the DGP calibrated to these
estimates is future work. A working protocol for it exists in the
repository, and it has not been run.

```{r planningg10data}
## Driver 19, --params published, blocks P and F (published-planning/)
## and block N (published-planning/block-N/); pub_ok(), pend() and
## rate_cmp() are defined in the fig4bg10data chunk.
pg_file <- pub_ok('planning-g10.csv')
pg9_file <- pub_ok('planning-g9.csv')
have_pg <- !is.na(pg_file) && !is.na(pg9_file)
if (have_pg) {
  pg <- read.csv(pg_file)
  pg9 <- read.csv(pg9_file)
  pg_key <- c('design', 'c_bm', 't_half', 'N_label')
  pg_vs9 <- merge(pg, pg9, by = pg_key, suffixes = c('', '_g9'))
  stopifnot(nrow(pg_vs9) == nrow(pg), nrow(pg) == nrow(pg9))
  pg_alt <- pg[pg$c_bm > 0, ]
  pg_n80 <- pg_alt[pg_alt$N_label == 'N80_E9' & !pg_alt$capped, ]
  pg_cap <- pg_alt[pg_alt$N_label == 'N80_E9' & pg_alt$capped, ]
}
pg_design <- c(Hybrid = 'Hybrid', `OL+BDC` = 'OL+BDC', Crossover = 'CO')
pg_cell <- function(d, cbm, th, nlab) {
  pg[pg$design == pg_design[d] & pg$c_bm == cbm & pg$t_half == th &
     pg$N_label == nlab, ]
}
pg_pow <- function(d, cbm, th, nlab = '70', dagger = TRUE) pend(have_pg, {
  r <- pg_cell(d, cbm, th, nlab)
  if (nrow(r) != 1) return('')
  paste0(sprintf('%.3f', r$power), if (dagger && r$capped) '$^\\dagger$' else '')
})
pg_mcse <- function(d, cbm, th, nlab = '70')
  pend(have_pg, sprintf('%.3f', pg_cell(d, cbm, th, nlab)$mcse))
fmt_range <- function(x) sprintf('%.3f to %.3f', min(x), max(x))
pg_vs9_max <- pend(have_pg,
  sprintf('%.3f', max(abs(pg_vs9$power - pg_vs9$power_g9))))
pg_size_range <- pend(have_pg, fmt_range(pg$size[!is.na(pg$size)]))
pg_size_mcse <- pend(have_pg, sprintf('%.3f', max(pg$mcse[pg$c_bm == 0])))
pg_size_reps <- pend(have_pg, format(max(pg$n_reps[pg$c_bm == 0]),
                                     big.mark = ','))
pg_alt_reps <- pend(have_pg, format(max(pg_alt$n_reps), big.mark = ','))
pg_alt_mcse <- pend(have_pg, sprintf('%.3f', max(pg_alt$mcse)))
pg_n80_range <- pend(have_pg, fmt_range(pg_n80$power))
pg_n80_n <- pend(have_pg, nrow(pg_n80))
pg_cap_range <- pend(have_pg, fmt_range(pg_cap$power))
pg_cap_n <- pend(have_pg, nrow(pg_cap))
## Uncapped cells only: a capped cell ran below the E9 sample size.
pg_min_n80 <- pend(have_pg, sprintf('%.3f', min(pg_n80$power)))
pg_nonconv_max <- pend(have_pg, sprintf('%.3f', max(pg$nonconv)))
pg_nonconv_pct <- pend(have_pg, sprintf('%.1f', 100 * max(pg$nonconv)))

## Closed-form E9 power at N = 70 (17-rho-stage.R, planning-n80.csv).
pn80 <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                           'carryover-closed-form', 'rho-stage',
                           'planning-n80.csv'))
e9_pow <- function(d, cbm, th) {
  v <- pn80$power_N70[pn80$design == pg_design[[d]] & pn80$c_bm == cbm &
                      pn80$t_half == th]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
e9_fmt <- function(d, cbm, th) sprintf('%.3f', e9_pow(d, cbm, th))
## G10 at N = 70 against closed-form E9, every alternative cell: counts
## of cells where G10 is more than two Monte Carlo SEs above, within,
## and below.
pg_vs_e9 <- if (have_pg) {
  a <- pg_alt[pg_alt$N_label == '70', ]
  e9 <- mapply(function(d, cb, th) {
    e9_pow(names(pg_design)[pg_design == d], cb, th)
  }, a$design, a$c_bm, a$t_half)
  z <- (a$power - e9) / a$mcse
  c(above = sum(z > 2), within = sum(abs(z) <= 2), below = sum(z < -2),
    cells = nrow(a))
} else NULL
pg_vs_e9_txt <- pend(have_pg, {
  k <- pg_vs_e9
  if (k[['above']] == k[['cells']]) {
    sprintf('higher power than E9 in every one of the %d cells', k[['cells']])
  } else {
    sprintf(paste('power more than two Monte Carlo SEs above that of E9 in',
                  '%d of the %d cells, within two SEs in %d and below in %d'),
            k[['above']], k[['cells']], k[['within']], k[['below']])
  }
})
## Is the closed-form E9 rule conservative for G10? At the E9 sample
## size, every uncapped cell must reach 0.80 within two Monte Carlo
## SEs.
pg_short <- if (have_pg) pg_n80[pg_n80$power < 0.8 - 2 * pg_n80$mcse, ] else NULL
pg_conservative <- have_pg && nrow(pg_short) == 0

## Block N: N for 80 percent power of G10 in the Hybrid design.
n80_dir <- file.path(pub_dir, 'block-N')
n80_file <- pub_ok('n80-g10.csv', n80_dir)
n80_meta_file <- pub_ok('meta.rds', n80_dir)
have_n80 <- !is.na(n80_file) && !is.na(n80_meta_file)
if (have_n80) {
  n80 <- read.csv(n80_file)
  n80_meta <- readRDS(n80_meta_file)
  n80_in <- n80[!n80$extrapolated, ]
}
n80_mult_txt <- pend(have_n80, sprintf('%g to %g',
  min(n80_meta$n80_mult), max(n80_meta$n80_mult)))
n80_k <- pend(have_n80, length(n80_meta$n80_mult))
n80_reps <- pend(have_n80, format(n80_meta$reps_n80, big.mark = ','))
n80_ratio_range <- pend(have_n80, if (nrow(n80_in) == 0) 'not estimable' else
  sprintf('%.2f to %.2f', min(n80_in$ratio_to_E9), max(n80_in$ratio_to_E9)))
n80_n_in <- pend(have_n80, nrow(n80_in))
n80_n_ex <- pend(have_n80, sum(n80$extrapolated))
```

**Sample size.** Table \@ref(tab:planning) gives the total $N$ for 80%
power of the paired-difference statistic E9 under the extended DGP, by
design, $c_{bm}$ and half-life, and the power at the original
$N = 70$. The sample sizes are closed-form values for E9. In the
Hybrid design E9 tracks the original mixed model closely (Methods). In
the crossover design it understates a time-adjusted mixed model. At
the pharmacological half-life the Hybrid design needs about 280
participants at $c_{bm} = 0.25$ and 84 at 0.45. At a 1-week half-life
those rise to 480 and 146. For comparison, Brookes et al.
[@brookes2004] found that a main-effect test needs about a quarter of
the sample of an interaction test of the same size. Their result is
for a binary subgroup with two equal halves. Carrying the factor to a
continuous biomarker slope of the same standardized size is an
extrapolation.

**The recommended analysis at the planned sample sizes.** The
companion paper [@pmsimstats-paper02] recommends the analysis G10 for
the interaction. G10 is a linear mixed model with a random intercept
and continuous-time AR(1) residual correlation. Its drug indicator is
the exposure-decayed $D_{bc}$ at an analysis half-life chosen by AIC
over 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 weeks. The selection uses maximum-likelihood
fits of the model without the interaction, so the choice of half-life
does not depend on the term under test. The model at the chosen
half-life is refitted by REML with the interaction, and the
interaction is tested with CR2 cluster-robust standard errors and
Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. We simulated G10 under the extended
DGP with the original parameters in every cell of Table
\@ref(tab:planning), at $N = 70$ and at the E9 sample size for 80
percent power, with `r pg_alt_reps` replicates per cell. We also
simulated the null ($c_{bm} = 0$) at $N = 70$ for each design and
half-life with `r pg_size_reps` replicates. The last column of Table
\@ref(tab:planning) gives G10 power at $N = 70$ at the 0.2-week
half-life, and Table \@ref(tab:planningg10) gives every cell. Where the
E9 sample size exceeded 400, or was above 800 and not computed, the
cell ran at $N = 400$ and is marked.

Three results follow. First, G10 rejected the null at
`r pg_size_range` across the nine design-by-half-life cells (Monte
Carlo SE at most `r pg_size_mcse`). Second, at $N = 70$ G10 has
`r pg_vs_e9_txt`. In the Hybrid design at $c_{bm} = 0.25$ and the
0.2-week half-life, G10 power is `r pg_pow('Hybrid', 0.25, 0.2)`
(MCSE `r pg_mcse('Hybrid', 0.25, 0.2)`) against
`r e9_fmt('Hybrid', 0.25, 0.2)` for E9. In the crossover design at the
same cell it is `r pg_pow('Crossover', 0.25, 0.2)` (MCSE
`r pg_mcse('Crossover', 0.25, 0.2)`) against
`r e9_fmt('Crossover', 0.25, 0.2)`. Third, at the E9 sample size for
80 percent power, G10 power is `r pg_n80_range` in the `r pg_n80_n`
uncapped cells, and `r pg_cap_range` in the `r pg_cap_n` cells that
ran at $N = 400$. `r if (!have_pg) PENDING else if (pg_conservative) paste0('The closed-form E9 rule is therefore conservative for G10: a trial sized by Table \\@ref(tab:planning) and analyzed with G10 had power of at least ', pg_min_n80, ' in every uncapped cell.') else sprintf('The closed-form E9 rule is therefore not conservative for G10 in every cell: in %d of the %d uncapped cells G10 power at the E9 sample size is more than two Monte Carlo SEs below 0.80.', nrow(pg_short), nrow(pg_n80))`
Fits failed to converge in at most `r pg_nonconv_max` of replicates in
any cell, and the rejection rates are computed over converged fits.

The same simulated trials were also analyzed with G9, which chooses
the half-life by AIC with the interaction in the model. In every cell
the G9 and G10 rejection rates differ by at most `r pg_vs9_max`.

**The sample size for G10.** In the nine Hybrid cells we simulated G10
at `r n80_k` multiples of the E9 sample size, from `r n80_mult_txt`
times, with `r n80_reps` replicates at each, and fitted a probit
regression of rejection on $\log N$ in each cell. Table
\@ref(tab:n80g10) gives the $N$ at which the fitted power is 0.80. `r if (have_n80 && sum(n80$extrapolated) == 0) paste0('That $N$ lies inside the simulated range in all ', n80_n_in, ' cells, and it is ', n80_ratio_range, ' times the E9 value.') else paste0('In the ', n80_n_in, ' cells where that $N$ lies inside the simulated range, it is ', n80_ratio_range, ' times the E9 value. In the remaining ', n80_n_ex, ' cells it lies outside the range, and the value is an extrapolation from the fitted curve and is marked.')` The E9 values are
closed form, so this comparison is the measured difference between
the paired-difference approximation and the analysis a trial would
use.

```{r planning}
tab <- data.frame(
  design = c('Hybrid', '', '', 'OL+BDC', '', '', 'Crossover', '', ''),
  cbm = rep(c(0.25, 0.35, 0.45), 3),
  slope = rep(c(2.0, 2.8, 3.6), 3),
  n0 = NA, n02 = NA, n1 = NA, p70 = NA)
pn80 <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                           'carryover-closed-form', 'rho-stage',
                           'planning-n80.csv'))
pn80_get <- function(col, th) {
  d <- rep(c('Hybrid', 'OL+BDC', 'CO'), each = 3)
  mapply(function(dd, cb) {
    v <- pn80[[col]][pn80$design == dd & pn80$c_bm == cb & pn80$t_half == th]
    stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
    v
  }, d, tab$cbm, USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}
pn80_n <- function(th) {
  v <- pn80_get('N80', th)
  ifelse(is.na(v), '> 800', as.character(v))
}
tab$n0 <- pn80_n(0)
tab$n02 <- pn80_n(0.2)
tab$n1 <- pn80_n(1)
tab$p70 <- round(pn80_get('power_N70', 0.2), 3)
tab$g70 <- mapply(function(d, cb) pg_pow(d, cb, 0.2, '70'),
                  rep(c('Hybrid', 'OL+BDC', 'Crossover'), each = 3), tab$cbm)
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, escape = FALSE, align = 'lrrrrrrr',
  linesep = '',
  col.names = c('Design', '$c_{bm}$', 'Slope (points per SD)', '$t_{1/2} = 0$', '0.2 week', '1 week', 'E9', 'G10'),
  caption = paste0('Planning under the extended DGP (separable AR(1), $\\rho = 0.7$, $c_1 = 0.2$, decaying correlation, carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean, original response parameters): total $N$ for 80 percent power of the paired-difference statistic E9 at $\\alpha = 0.05$, by design, interaction strength and carryover half-life, with the implied slope in symptom points per SD of biomarker ($\\sigma_{BR} = 8$) and the power at $N = 70$ and the 0.2-week half-life for E9 (closed form) and for the analysis G10 (simulated, ', pg_alt_reps, ' replicates per cell, Monte Carlo SE at most ', pg_alt_mcse, '). Participants are allocated to paths in the original fixed proportions.')) |>
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(' ' = 3, 'N for 80 percent power' = 3, 'Power at $N = 70$, 0.2 week' = 2), escape = FALSE)
```

G10 was simulated at ', n80_k, ' values of $N$ per cell (', n80_reps, ' replicates each), and the $N$ at which a probit regression of rejection on $\\log N$ reaches 0.80 is rounded up. $\\ddagger$: outside the simulated range of $N$, an extrapolation. n/e: the fitted curve does not rise with $N$.'))
```

**Parameters by status.**

- *Original values:* the Gompertz parameters of the three components
  and their standard deviations; the biomarker and baseline means and
  standard deviations; $c_1 = 0.2$; the path allocation; the
  expectancy values; the restart of time on drug at re-exposure.
- *Chosen here:* the decaying correlation and the stop on infeasible
  matrices (the extensions); carryover decaying from the last on-drug
  mean; AR(1) in weeks with $\rho = 0.7$; the separable
  cross-component form; the symptom half-life range of 0.1 to 0.2
  week; the option defaults used in the stress test.
- *Uncalibrated:* every value above. None was re-estimated for this
  paper. CSP 563 estimates the baseline and biomarker SDs, the total
  placebo-arm improvement and the total-score covariance, and it does
  not identify the component split, the expectancy weight or the
  half-life (above). The values to which the results are most
  sensitive are $\rho$ (Stage 4), $\sigma_{BR}$ (which sets the slope a
  given $c_{bm}$ implies) and the half-life.

**Choosing $c_{bm}$.** Take the smallest feasibility bound over the
designs and half-lives in the study (Table \@ref(tab:ceilings) and
Appendix A.5; 0.474 for the three designs at $\rho = 0.7$ without
carryover, higher with carryover). State $c_{bm}$ as a slope in
outcome points per SD of biomarker. Keep it below that bound. The
package reports an infeasible value by stopping.

# Discussion

## The correlation encoding of the interaction

**Conditional structure.** Under joint normality, conditioning on the
biomarker shows what the correlation encoding does to the drug
response. With $b_i$ the standardized biomarker,

$$
E(BR_{it} \mid B_i) = \mu_{BR,t} + c_{bm}\, g_t\, \sigma_{BR}\, b_i,
\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(BR_{i\cdot} \mid B_i) = \Sigma_{BR} - c_{bm}^2\sigma_{BR}^2\, g g^\top .
$$

The encoding therefore shifts the conditional drug-response mean in
proportion to the correlation profile $g_t$. It reduces the residual
drug-response covariance by a rank-one term. Two consequences follow.

- **The power loss under carryover is set by the profile.** The size
  of the loss depends on whether the interaction fades with the drug
  effect, which is the correlation rule.
- **The feasibility bound is the condition** that the reduced
  residual covariance remains positive definite.

The contribution of the original DGP is therefore a parameterization
of the interaction as a correlation that keeps the marginal variance
of the drug response fixed. We found no earlier use of that
parameterization in the N-of-1 literature we searched (Background).
Both its strengths and its limits
follow from it.

The correlation encoding has four strengths.

- **One interpretable parameter.** The interaction strength is a
  single correlation. Its square, $c_{bm}^2$, is the share of on-drug
  drug-response variance the biomarker explains.
- **A reduced form of responder heterogeneity.** Suppose participants
  fall into two latent responder classes, and both the biomarker and
  the drug response differ between classes. Then class membership
  carries the covariance between them. Matching second moments gives
  $c_{bm}^2 = f_B f_{BR}$, where $f_B$ and $f_{BR}$ are the fractions
  of the biomarker's and the drug response's variance that lie between
  classes (Appendix A.6). The encoding therefore matches the second
  moments of a responder-class mechanism without requiring the mixture
  to be identified. Identifying the mixture typically needs larger
  samples than N-of-1 programs enroll
  [@bauercurran2003; @lubkemuthen2005; @nylund2007]. The match
  is limited to second moments. The mixture's conditional mean is
  nonlinear in the biomarker, and its higher moments differ.
- **The marginal variance of the drug response is fixed.** The
  biomarker explains part of the existing variation rather than
  adding to it. The effect size can therefore be stated as a share of
  response variance without changing the response distribution.
- **It fits a biomarker that marks individual sensitivity to the
  drug** better than one that sets a fixed dose-response shift.

It also has four structural limits.

- **The joint distribution must exist,** which bounds the effect size.
  In outcome units the bound is $c_{bm}^{*}\sigma_{BR}$ per SD of
  biomarker, 3.8 points under the extended DGP at the original
  $\sigma_{BR}$. The planning section shows this is below the
  association first reported for prazosin, which did not replicate in
  CSP 563. The bound depends on the correlation structure
  and the design.
- **The correlation must be specified at off-drug visits.** A constant
  correlation after first exposure removes the interaction under
  carryover. The specification adopted here is itself asymmetric
  between titration and washout (Stage 2).
- **The drug-response component keeps its full variance at off-drug
  visits,** with zero mean. This adds noise to every on-off contrast.
  It belongs to the component decomposition, not to the correlation
  encoding.
- **A correlation is less intuitive than a slope for clinical
  readers.** The slope it implies, $-c_{bm}\sigma_{BR}/\sigma_{bm}$,
  must be derived before it can be compared with an observed effect.
  The comparison depends on $\sigma_{BR}$, which is not estimated.

A model that generates the drug response from a participant-level
sensitivity to exposure would address these limits:

$$
BR_{it} = \omega_i f(t) + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad
\omega_i = \bar\omega\,(1 + \zeta b_i) + u_i ,
$$

where $f(t)$ is the exposure-response time course, $\zeta$ the
biomarker's effect on sensitivity and $u_i$ the sensitivity it does
not explain. This is a random-coefficient model with a
covariate-by-exposure interaction, the form used to describe
individual response in replicated crossover and N-of-1 trials
[@senn2016mastering; @araujo2016].

- It encodes the biomarker through individual sensitivity, so it has
  no feasibility bound.
- Its moderation is proportional to the response at every visit, so it
  fades during titration as well as after discontinuation.
- Its off-drug variance shrinks with the response.

It is not yet implemented in the software. Its response half-life for
prazosin in PTSD is not known. Until then, the correlation encoding's
range of use is effect sizes below the feasibility bound, which the
planning section translates into outcome units.

## What remains uncalibrated

The extended DGP meets the existence, identifiability and
analyzability criteria by construction and derivation. It meets the
fidelity criterion by judgment. It does not meet the calibration
criterion: every parameter is the original value or a choice made
here. The values that matter most are the serial correlation, the
drug-response SD and the symptom half-life. The parallel-group trial
CSP 563 informs only the first, and only on the total score. Its CAPS
correlation decays slowly, compound symmetry fits it worst among the
structures compared, and the DGP's total-score correlation decays
faster at short lags (planning section). All three values could be
estimated from an aggregated N-of-1 trial of prazosin with weekly
symptom measurement. Such a trial would also show which correlation
form fits weekly series.

## Recommendations

For simulation studies that build on the original DGP, we recommend
the following.

1. **Apply both extensions:** stop on non-positive-definite matrices,
   and let the biomarker-response correlation decay after
   discontinuation.
2. **State the choices:** carryover decaying from the last on-drug
   mean, AR(1) in weeks at a reported $\rho$, and the separable
   cross-component form. Repeat the analysis at neighboring $\rho$
   where the conclusion could depend on it.
3. **Choose $c_{bm}$ below the feasibility bound** for every design in
   the study. Report it on two scales: as $c_{bm}$, and as the implied
   slope in outcome points per SD of biomarker.
4. **Keep the original DGP as a reference arm** whenever results are
   compared with the original ones. Attribute each difference to a
   named stage.
5. **Include a prognostic scenario** whenever the analysis shares the
   biomarker effect with the baseline visit. State the trade-off
   between the power of the plain model and the robustness of the
   expectancy-term model rather than resolving it for the trialist.
6. **Use the sensitivity model, once available, for effects above the
   feasibility bound.** Until then, state the bound in outcome units
   as a limitation.

## Limitations

- **The closed form covers one statistic.** It is exact for the
  paired-difference statistic, not for the original mixed model. The
  two agree closely in the Hybrid design. In the crossover design the
  closed form understates what a time-adjusted analysis achieves. The
  sample sizes of the planning table inherit this. The simulated G10
  columns show the direction and size of the difference: at the E9
  sample size G10 power was `r pg_n80_range` in the uncapped cells. The
  G10 sample size for 80 percent power was searched for in the Hybrid
  design only, by simulation at `r n80_k` values of $N$ per cell, and
  it carries Monte Carlo error that Table \@ref(tab:n80g10) does not
  show.
- **At pharmacological half-lives the extended DGP shows no carryover
  effect.** The on/off correlation difference is within 0.01 of 1 at
  0.2 week. The DGP therefore tests carryover only at half-lives of
  0.5 week and above, which we cannot ground pharmacologically.
- **The correlation is asymmetric between titration and washout.**
  Full moderation during the first weeks on drug is a modeling choice
  inherited from the original DGP, not a consequence of the
  pharmacology.
- **Parameter values are not estimated.** The Gompertz parameters,
  correlations, $\sigma_{BR}$ and prognostic correlations are original
  values or chosen values. A reanalysis of CSP 563 estimates the
  total-score variance and correlation, which differ from the DGP's,
  and cannot identify the component split, the expectancy weight or
  the half-life. The motivating blood-pressure association did not
  replicate there.
- **The DGP is Gaussian with a single biomarker.**
- **The pharmacological carryover range** for prazosin at weekly
  visits is inferred from its plasma half-life, not measured as a
  symptom-response half-life.
- **The stress test is exploratory.** Cells and analyses were added
  after first results. Its prognostic scenarios are the ones that show
  the size inflation by construction.

# Conclusions

The original DGP encodes the predictive-biomarker interaction as a
correlation between the biomarker and the drug response. That encoding
remains a coherent choice for simulating aggregated N-of-1 trials. The
original DGP holds the correlation constant after first exposure, so
the interaction is absent whenever there is carryover. It repairs
correlation matrices that are not positive definite. Both features
have closed-form explanations, and both are changed by small
extensions. With a correlation that decays after discontinuation and
a feasibility check that stops instead of repairing, the extended DGP
returns the no-carryover power at pharmacological half-lives (the
on/off correlation difference is within 0.01 of 1 at 0.2 week). Power
declines smoothly at half-lives of 0.5 week and above. The decline is
proved monotone for the path-stratified paired-difference statistic
and was checked on a grid for the pooled statistic. A serial
correlation of 0.7 and a separable AR(1) structure allow a
biomarker-response correlation of 0.47, or 3.8 symptom points per SD
of biomarker at the original drug-response SD. The planning table
quantifies the power at matched strength, for the paired-difference
statistic in closed form and for the recommended mixed-model analysis
G10 by simulation. At the closed-form sample size, G10 power was
`r pg_n80_range` in the uncapped cells, and in the Hybrid design the
G10 sample size for 80 percent power was `r n80_ratio_range` times the
closed-form value where it could be located. We propose the extended
DGP,
with options for prognostic pathways and other features that change
which analysis is valid, as the reference for simulation studies of
these designs. Every parameter is labeled as original, chosen or
uncalibrated.

# Glossary {-}

Terms are listed in the order in which the paper introduces them.
Labels in backticks are the identifiers used in the repository's
code, data files and table headings.

- **Original DGP** (`published` in code and data labels):
  the data-generating process of Hendrickson et al. (2020), as
  implemented in their code at commit 58b32a9.
- **Extended DGP** (`refined` in code and data labels): the
  data-generating process of Table \@ref(tab:spec), which adds the
  decaying correlation, the feasibility check, carryover decaying from
  the last on-drug mean, the separable AR(1) structure and the
  optional features to the original DGP.
- **Correlation encoding of the interaction** (`mvn`): the predictive
  biomarker is a correlation between the biomarker and the drug
  response that is present on drug and absent off drug.
- **Biomarker-response correlation** ($c_{bm}$, `c.bm`): the
  correlation between the baseline biomarker and the drug-response
  component at an on-drug visit, which sets the strength of the
  interaction.
- **Correlation profile** ($g_t$): the fraction of $c_{bm}$ present at
  visit $t$, equal to 1 on drug.
- **Original rule** (`step` in code and data labels): the
  biomarker-response correlation is $c_{bm}$ at every visit where the
  drug-response mean is nonzero, and so is constant after first
  exposure.
- **Decaying correlation** (`graded` in code and data labels): the
  extended rule, under which the correlation is $c_{bm}$ on drug,
  $c_{bm}2^{-t_{sd}/t_{1/2}}$ off drug after exposure, and 0 before
  exposure.
- **On/off correlation difference** ($\mathcal G$): the on-drug value
  of $g_t$ minus the mean of $g_t$ over the post-baseline off-drug
  visits, $1 - \bar g_{\text{off}}$, through which alone the
  correlation rule affects closed-form power.
- **Feasibility bound** ($c_{bm}^{*}$, "Ceiling" in tables): the
  largest $c_{bm}$ for which the correlation matrix is positive
  definite under a given correlation structure, design and
  correlation profile.
- **Carryover half-life** ($t_{1/2}$, `carryover_t1half`): the time
  after discontinuation for the drug-response mean, and under the
  extended rule the biomarker-response correlation, to fall by half.
- **Pharmacological and behavioral half-lives**: half-lives of 0.1 to
  0.2 week are the assumed pharmacological range for prazosin, and
  half-lives of 0.5 week and above are labeled behavioral scenarios.
- **Original carryover rule** (`recursive`): the drug-response mean at
  an off-drug visit is the previous visit's mean decayed by the time
  since discontinuation, so the decay compounds across visits.
- **Extended carryover rule** (`anchored`): the drug-response mean at
  an off-drug visit is the last on-drug mean decayed by the elapsed
  time since discontinuation.
- **Drug-response component** (BR): the latent response driven by time
  on drug, with mean on a modified Gompertz curve.
- **Placebo-response component** (PB): the latent response driven by
  time in the trial and scaled by the expectancy.
- **Natural-history component** (TV): the latent response driven by
  time in the trial that does not depend on treatment.
- **Baseline severity** (BL): the participant's symptom level before
  any response, which enters every visit equally.
- **Expectancy** ($\eta_t$): the participant's probability of being on
  drug at visit $t$ given the design, 1 in the open-label phase and
  0.5 when blinded.
- **Compound symmetry** ($\rho_{cs}$): the same correlation between
  any two visits of a component, whatever their separation.
- **Separable AR(1) structure**: the same first-order autoregressive
  correlation $\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$ for every component,
  with a constant between-component correlation $c_1$ at every lag,
  so that the response block is a Kronecker product.
- **Two-constant form**: an AR(1) structure in which the same-visit
  cross-component correlation $c_1$ and the other-visit correlation
  $c_\times\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$ use different constants.
- **Hybrid design** (`Hybrid`): open-label titration, blinded
  discontinuation, then a brief crossover, with visits at weeks 4, 8,
  9, 10, 11, 12, 16 and 20.
- **OL+BDC** (`OLBDC`): open label followed by blinded
  discontinuation.
- **CO**: the crossover design, in which participants receive drug and
  placebo in one of two orders.
- **OL**: the open-label design, in which every visit is on drug.
- **Path**: one sequence of drug and placebo phases within a design,
  to which participants are allocated in fixed numbers.
- **Paired-difference statistic** (E9, E9b): the per-participant
  difference between the mean on-drug and mean off-drug scores,
  regressed on the biomarker, using post-baseline visits only (E9) or
  counting baseline as one more off-drug visit (E9b).
- **Original analysis**: the linear mixed
  model of the original study, with a random intercept, a binary drug
  indicator and baseline included as an off-drug row.
- **G10** (`E7null_cr2` in data labels): the analysis the companion
  paper recommends; a random-intercept CAR(1) mixed model with the
  exposure-decayed drug indicator at a half-life chosen by AIC over
  0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 weeks from maximum-likelihood fits without the
  interaction, refitted by REML with the interaction, with CR2
  cluster-robust standard errors and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.
- **G9** (`E7cr2` in data labels): as G10, except that the half-life is
  chosen with the interaction in the model.
- **Capped cell** ($\dagger$ in Table \@ref(tab:planningg10)): a cell
  whose E9 sample size for 80 percent power exceeds 400, simulated at
  $N = 400$.
- **Exposure-decayed drug indicator** ($D_{bc}$): a drug indicator
  equal to 1 on drug, $2^{-t_{sd}/t_{1/2}}$ off drug after exposure,
  and 0 before exposure.
- **Prognostic correlation** ($c_{PB}$, $c_{TV}$, $c_{BL}$;
  `prog-PB`, `prog-TV-const`, `prog-TV-grow`, `prog-BL` in data
  labels): a correlation of the biomarker with the placebo-response
  component, with the natural-history component (constant over visits,
  or growing along its curve), or with baseline severity.
- **Expectancy-term model**: the random-intercept CAR(1) analysis that
  adds the expectancy and a biomarker-by-expectancy term to the mean
  model.
- **Free-baseline model**: the random-intercept CAR(1) analysis that
  adds `bmc:bl0`, a separate biomarker slope for the baseline row.
- **CAR(1)**: the continuous-time first-order autoregressive residual
  correlation `corCAR1` of the analysis model.
- **Calibration ratio** ($\kappa$): the mean model standard error
  divided by the empirical standard deviation of the estimates.
- **Stress test** (`11-strawman-stress-test.R`): study 3, the
  simulation that fits fourteen analyses to trials from the extended
  DGP with and without a prognostic biomarker.
- **First and second runs of the stress test** (`summary-full*.csv`
  and `summary-full*-anchored.csv`): the first run used the original
  carryover rule (`recursive`) and fixed allocation. The second run,
  reported in Stage 6, used carryover decaying from the last on-drug
  mean (`anchored`) and randomized allocation.
- **The five criteria**: existence (the joint distribution exists),
  identifiability under carryover (the interaction remains an
  on-minus-off contrast), fidelity to the pharmacology, analyzability
  (the analysis model can represent the generated structure and the
  DGP can generate the features that decide validity), and
  calibration status (each parameter is labeled original, chosen or
  uncalibrated).

# Abbreviations {-}

ADEMP: aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods,
performance measures; AIC: Akaike information criterion; BDC:
blinded discontinuation; BL: baseline
severity; BR: drug-response component; CAPS: Clinician-Administered
PTSD Scale; CAR(1): continuous-time first-order autoregressive
correlation; CO: crossover; CR2: bias-reduced cluster-robust variance
estimator; CS: compound symmetry; DGP: data-generating process; E9,
E9b: the paired-difference interaction statistic on post-baseline
visits, and with baseline counted as an off-drug visit; MCSE: Monte
Carlo standard error; OL: open label; OL+BDC: open label followed by
blinded discontinuation; PB: placebo-response component; PD: positive
definite; PTSD: post-traumatic stress disorder; TV: natural-history
component.
